MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, in pursuance of the Directions of an Act, passed in the 24th year of His present Majesty, he had issued his Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown to make out new Writs for the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the following Places; viz. for the Borough of Yarmouth, in the County of Southampton, in the room of Charles Mac Donnelly Esquire,

deceased; and for the County of in the room of

the Moll honourable Henry Charles Somerset, commonly called Marquis of Worcester, now Duke of , called up to the House of Peers.

Several Members present, and several Members returned upon New Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Outlawries, was read the firftTime.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had this day attended His Majesty, in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent mistakes, obtained a copy; which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Since I last met you in Parliament, it has been my chief object to carry into eflfcdl those measures which your wisdom had adopted for the Defence of the United Kingdom, and for the vigorous prosecution of the War. In these preparations I have been seconded by the voluntary Vo t. 59.

exertions of all ranks of My People, in a manner that has, if possible, strengthened their claims to My confidence and affection; they have proved, that the menaces of the Enemy have only served to rouse their native and hereditary spirit i and that all other considerations are loft in a general disposition to make those efforts and sacrifices, which the honour and safety of the Kingdom demand at this important and critical conjuncture.

Though my attention has principally been directed to the great object of internal security, no opportunity has been loft of making an impression on the Foreign possessions of the Enemy. The Islands of Saint Lucia, of fob ago, of Saint Pierre, and Miquelon, and the Settlements of Denier ar a and Efequibo, have surrendered to the British arms. In the conduct of the operations by which those valuable acquisitions have been made, the utmost promptitude and zeal have been displayed by the Officers employed on those services, and by My Forces acting under their command by sea and land.

In Ireland, the leaders, and several inferior agents, in the late traitorous and atrocious conspiracy, have been brought to justice; and the public tranquillity has experienced no further interruption. I indulge the hope, that such of My deluded Subjects as have swerved from their allegiance are now convinced of their error; and "that, having compared the advantages they derive from the protection of a free constitution, with the condition of those countries which are under the dominion of the French Government, they will cordially and zealously concur in refilling any attempt that may be made against the security and independence of My United Kingdom.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have a perfect reliance on your public spirit for making such provision as may be necessary for the Service of the year. The progressive improvement of the Revenue cannot fail to encourage you to persevere in the lyftem which has been adopted, of defraying the Expences of the War, with as little addition as possible to the Public Debt, and to the permanent burthens of the State.

I lament the heavy prefi'ure which, under the present circumstances, mull unavoidably be experienced by My People; but I am persuaded that they will meet it" with the good l'enfe and fortitude which so eminently distinguish their character, under a conviction of the indispensible importance of upholding the dignity, and of providing effectually for the lafety, of the Empire.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have concluded a Convention with the King of Sweden, for the purpose of adjusting all the differences which have arilen on the subject of the Eleventh Article of the Treaty

* ‘ of

22° Novembris* A. 1803*

of 1661. I have directed that a Copy of this Convention should be laid before you; and you will, I trust, be of Opinion that the arrangement, whilst it upholds our Maritime Rights, is founded on those principles of reciprocal - advantage which are best calculated to maintain and improve the good understanding which happily subsists between the two Countries.

In the prosecution of the contest in which we arc engaged, it shall be, as it has ever been, My first object to execute as becomes Me the great trust committed to My charge. Embarked with My brave and loyal People in one common cause, it is my fixed determination, if the occasion should arise, to share their exertions and their dangers, in the defence of Our Constitution, Our Religion, Our Laws, and Independence. To the activity and valour of My Fleets and Armies, to the zeal and unconquerable spirit of My faithful Subjects, I confide the honour of My Crown, and all those valuable interests which are involved in the issue of this momentous contest.

Actuated by these sentiments, and humbly imploring the blessing of Divine Providence, I look forward with a firm conviction, that if, contrary to all just expectation, the Enemy should elude the vigilance of my numerous Fleets and Cruizers, and attempt to execute their presumptuous threat of invading Our coasts, the consequences will be to them discomfiture, confusion, and disgrace; and that Our’s will not only be the glory of surmounting present difficulties, and repelling immediate danger, but the (olid , and permanent advantage of fixing the safety and independence of the Kingdom on the basis of acknowledged strength, the result of its own tried energy and resources.

To allure His Majesty, that this House are deeply fen-fible of His Majesty’s paternal care, and attention to the safety and interests of His faithful people, in carrying into effect such measures as Parliament has adopted for the defence of the United Kingdom, and the vigorous prosecution of the War:

That it is highly gratifying to this House to reflect, that in those preparations His Majesty has been seconded by the Voluntary exertions of all ranks of His People, in a manner , - which His Majesty has been most graciously pleased to

declare, has, if possible, strengthened their claims to his Confidence and affection:

That they feel with just exultation, that the menaces of the Enemy have only served to rouse the native and hereditary spirit of this Nation, and that all other considerations are loft in a general disposition to make those efforts and sacrifices, which the honour and safety of the Kingdom demand at this important and critical conjuncture: Humbly to congratulate His Majesty on the impression which, notwithstanding the necessity of principally attending to the great object of internal security, has been made on the Foreign possessions of the Enemy, by the capture of the I!stands of St. Lucia, Tobago, St. Pierre, and Miquelon, and of the Settlements of Demerara and EJfequibe; and they are fully sensible of the promptitude and zeal displayed by the Officers employed in the conduct of the operations by which those valuable acquisitions have been made, and by the Forces acting under their command by sea and land:

To assure His Majesty, that they have great satisfaction in reflecting, that the leaders, and several of the inferior agents, in the late traitorous and atrocious conspiracy in Ireland, have been brought to justice; and that the public tranquillity has experienced no further interruption; and they earnestly participate in the hope which His Majesty has so graciously expressed, that such of His deluded Subjects as have swerved from their allegiance are now convinced of their error; and comparing the advantages they enjoy, under the protection of a free constitution, with the condition of the countries under the dominion of the French Government, they will cordially and zealously concur in refilling any attempt that may be made against the security and independence of the United Kingdom:

That they feel a perfect confidence that their fellow subjects will meet with fortitude the pressure, which the present situation of the Country renders unavoidable, under a conviction of the indispensible importance of upholding the dignity, and of providing effectually for the safety, of the Empire: ,

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath procured himself to be eletted or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any person hath been tampering with any witness, in respect of his evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing, or giving evidence, the fame is declared to be a high crime and misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath given false evidence, in any case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the ytmost severity against fuel? offender.

Resolved, That, in all cases of controverted elections for Counties in England and Wa, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their agents, within a convenient time, to be appointed by the House,deliver to the fitting Members, or their agents; Lifts of the persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the fitting Members j giving in the fold Lifts, the several heads of objection, and distinguishing the fame against the names of the voters excepted to; and that the fitting Members do, by themselves, or by their agents, within the same time, deliver the like Lifts on their part to the Petitioners, or their agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no person, so taken into custody, be discharged out of custody without the (pedal order of the House.

Ordered, That the back door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up, every Morning at the fitting of the House, and the key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any person whatsoever without order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every day before the door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from eleven of the clock in the Morning till one in the Afternoon, and from four till fix in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no obstru<ftions be made, by cars, drays, carts, or otherwise, to hinder the passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give notice of this order to the officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care that there be no gaming or other disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the passages leading to the House, during the fitting of Parliament;and that there be no annoyance by chairmen, footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of W ejlminster; and that he do fee the same put in execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the lobby of the House, or upon the stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do take care that there be no gaming, or other disorders, in the room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of custody but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of letters direifted to Members of this House, the person appointed to bring letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other person, to be appointed by the Post Master General, do, for the future, every day during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from ten of the clock in the Morning till one in the Afternoon, and for two hours at the least immediately after the rising of the House; and also from five of the clock in the Afternoon till seven, at the place appointed for the delivery of the said letters, and take care, during his stay there; to deliver the same to the several Members to whom theylhall be directed, or to their known servant or servants, or others, bringing notes under the hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such letters as shall remain undelivered, and that no letter be delivered but within the hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Post Master General.

Ordered, That when any Let ter or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the same; and acquaint the House, at their next fitting, with the contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give notice thereof to all Committees; and that 1

all proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being firftperufed by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the printing thereof; and that no person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to enquire Committee#* what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report Laws ' 5 their Opinion, from time to time, to the House, which of appointed, them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual:

The House was moved, That the Petition of Esquire, which was presented to this House upon the 27th day of May, in the last Session of Parliament, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Thomas Fydell, the younger, Esquire, for the Borough of , in the County of Lincoln, in which Petition the qualification of Mr. Fydell

is questioned by the Petitioner, might be read.

And the fame was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, That the entry in the Journal of the House, of the 5th day of December 1747, of the proceedings of the House, in relation to Matthew Michell, Esquire, who had petitioned this House,complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Westbury, in the County of Wilts, and whose qualification was questioned by the fitting Members, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

And the House being informed, that Mr. Fydell was, at the time of presenting the said Petition, out of this Kingdom, in Foreign parts, from whence he did not return till the beginning of this present month of November, when he was for the first time informed of the contents of the said Petition; and that therefore he could not comply with the Orders of the House of the 2 lft day of November 1717, relating to Qualifications;

Resolved, That the said Mr. Fydell be allowed seven days more, from this day, to leave with the Clerk of this House, an Account, in writing, of his qualification, as directed by the Orders of the House.

A Petition of several Proprietors of Lands in the Open and Common Fields of Kettering, in the County of North-

ampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Lands lie intermixed and dispersed, and are in their present state incapable of any considerable improvement: And therefore praying. That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for inclosing the said Open and Common Fields.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Cartwright and Mr. Dickins do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Several renewed Petitions, complaining of undue Elections and Returns, being offered to be presented to the House;

The House was moved, That the entry in the Journal of the House, of the 24th day of November, in the last Session of Parliament, of the Resolution of the House, directing the order in which Petitions complaining of undue Elections and Returns presented to this House, at the same time, shall be classed, might be read.

And the fame was read accordingly; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That whenever several Petitions, complaining " of undue Elections and Returns of Members to serve in " Parliament, shall, at the same time, be offered to be pre-" fented to the House, Mr. Speaker shall direct such Peti-" tions to be all of them delivered in at the Table, where " they shall be classed.and read in the following order; viz.

" Such Petitions as complain that no Return has been *• made of a Member or Members to serve in Parliament, in the first Class:

*Such as complain of Double Returns, in the second Class:

•* Such as complain of the Election or Return of Mem-<f bers returned to serve for two or more places, in the " third Class:

" Such as complain of Returns only, in the fourth Class: And,

" The Residue of the said Petitions, in the fifth Class."

Resolved, That whenever several renewed Petitions, complaining of undue Elections and Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, shall, at the same time, be offered to be presented to the House, Mr. Speaker shall direct such Petitions to be all of them delivered in at the Table; and the said Petitions shall be read in the order of the Classes mentioned in the said Resolution, and, in each of the Classes, in the order in which they were directed to be taken into consideration in the last Session of Parliament.

And several Petitions were accordingly delivered in at the Table, being all of them Petitions of the last Class mentioned in the Resolution of the House; and the fame were read by the Clerk, in the following order.

Mr. Ashley reported from the Committee, appointed yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty., That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the fame in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the tame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mott gracious Sovereign,

We Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg leave to return Your Majesty the thanks of this House, for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We allure Your Majesty, that we are deeply fenlible of Your Majesty’s paternal care, and attention to the safety and interests of Your faithful People, in carrying into effect tuch measures as Parliament has adopted for the defence of the United Kingdom, and the vigorous prosecution of the war.

We are highly gratified in refleding, that in those preparations Your Majesty has been seconded by the voluntary exertions of all ranks of Your People, in a manner which Your Majesty has been most graciously pleased to declare, has, if possible, strengthened their claims to Your Majesty’s confidence and affection.

We feel with just exultation, that-the menaces of the Enemy have only served to route the native and hereditary spirit of this Nation; and that all other considerations are loft in a general disposition to make those efforts and lacri-fices, which the honour and safety of the Kingdom demand at this important and critical conjundture.

We beg leave humbly to congratulate Your Majesty On the impression, which, notwithstanding the necelfity of principally attending to the great object of internal security, has been made on the Foreign Possessions of the Enemy, by the capture of the Islands of St. , , St.

and. Miquelon, and of the Settlements of and

EJJiequibo; and, we are fully fenlible of the promptitude and zeal displayed by the Officers employed in the conduct of the operations by which those valuable acquisitions have been, made, and by the forces acting under their command by sea and land.

We have great satisfaction in reflecting that the leaders, and several of the inferior agents, in the late traitorous and atrocious conspiracy in Ireland, have been brought to justice; and that the public tranquillity has experienced no further interruption; and we earnestly participate in the hope which Your Majesty has so graciously expressed, that such of Your Majesty’s deluded Subjects as have swerved from their allegiance, are now convinced of their error, and comparing the advantages they enjoy under the protect ion of a free constitution, with the condition of the countries under the dominion of the French Government, they will cordially and zealoully concur in refitting any attempt that may be made against the security and independence of the United Kingdom.

We assure Your Majesty, that You may rely on the readiness of Your faithful Commons to make such provision as may be necessary for the service of the year; and that we are fully sensible of the importance of persevering in the system which has been adopted, of defraying the expences of the War, with as little addition as possible to the Public Debt, and to the permanent burthens of the State.

We feel a perfect confidence that our fellow subjects will meet with fortitude the pressure, which the present situation of the Country renders unavoidable, under a

VOL. 59.

conviction of the indispensible importance of upholding tlfe dignity, and of providing effectually for the safety of the Empire.

We return our thanks to Your Majesty, for Your Majesty’s gracious intention of laying before us the Convention •which Your Majesty has concluded with the King of Sweden, for the purpose of adjusting the differences which have arisen on the subject of the Eleventh Article of the Treaty of 1661; and we trust that it will be found at once to uphold our Maritime Rights, and to produce the effect of maintaining and improving the good understanding which happily subsists between the two Countries.

We are most deeply convinced, that it will be, as it ever has been, Your Majesty’s first object to execute, as becomes Yout Royal Dignity, the great trust with which Your Majestyis invested; and we receive, with the strongest feelings of veneration and dutiful attachment, the expression of those paternal sentiments which induce Your Majesty to consider Yourself as embarked in one common cause with Your People, and which have determined Your Majesty, if the occasion should arise, to share their exertions and their dangers in the defence of our Constitution, our Religion, our Laws, and Independence.

We beg leave humbly to assure Your Majesty, that these sentiments will not be loft on an affectionate and grateful People, but will animate and invigorate the activity and valour of Your Majesty’s Fleets and Armies, and the zeal and determination of Ypur faithful Subjects, to which Your Majesty, under the protection of Divine Providence, may safely confide the honour of Your Crown, and all those important interests which are involved in the issue of this momentous contest.

Partaking of these Your Majesty’s sentiments, and joining with Your Majesty in humbly imploring the blessing of Divine Providence, we look forward with a firm conviction, that if, contrary to all'just expectation, the Enemy should elude the vigilance of Your Majesty’s Fleets and Cruisers, and attempt to execute their presumptuous threat of invading the jeoafts of the United Kingdom, the consequences will be to them difeomfiture, confusion, and disgrace'; and that the exertions of this kingdom will be rewarded, not only by the glory of surmounting present difficulties, and repelling immediate danger, but by the solid and permanent advantage of fixing its safety and independence on the basis of acknowledged strength, the result of its own tried energy and resources.

That at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough and Town of Wymouth and Melcombe Regis, in the County of Dorset, Sir James Pulteney, Baronet, Gabriel Tucker Steward, Esquire, Charles Adams, Esquire, William Garthjhore , Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates j and that at the said election a majority of legal votes were offered in favour of the Petitioner, but Thomas Morris, Esquire, the Mayor of the said Borough and Town, who presided as the Returning Officer at the said election, received the votes of many persons on the poll in favour of the said Charles Adams who had no right to vote at the said election, and rejected many legal votes which were tendered in favour of the Petitioner, by which means a majority appeared on the poll in favour of the said Charles Adams, and the said Thomas Morris hath unjustly returned the said Charles Adams duly elected; whereas the Petitioner had a majority of legal votes, and was duly elected, and ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House will take the premises into their consideration, and grant him such relief as they shall think proper.

APETITION of Henry Fane, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Fulbeck, in the County of Lincoln, and of several other Persons, Owners of Property within the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That there are within the said Parish certain Open Fields, Heath, Commonable, and Waste Lands, containing together 1,300 acres, or thereabouts, and also divers ancient inclosed Lands, containing upwards of 2,000 acres; and that it would be of great advantage to all parties concerned, if the said Open Fields, Heath, Commonable, and Waste Lands, were to be inclosed, and if the said inclosed Lands were discharged of Tythes, by an adequate compensation to the Rector in lieu thereof: And therefore praying. That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

That the retour referred to in the said claim, and produced to the meeting of Freeholders, did not afford sufficient legal evidence of the separate old extent of the Lands of Easter Glenboig, Mill, Mill Lands, and aftridted Multures, exclu-fively of the Office of Coroner, or Crownarie of the said Shire of Stirling; and that, notwithstanding these objections, a majority of the Freeholders present at the said meeting, determined that the said Charles Elphinstone Fleeming ought to be enrolled as a Freeholder of the said County at Stirling, and his name was accordingly added to the roll of Freeholders of the said Shire; and that, in the subsequent proceedings of the said meeting, held on the aforesaid 19th of July, 1802, the Petitioner and the said Charles Elphinstone Fleeming were the only Candidates for representing the said County of Stirling in Parliament; and that, previous to the roll being called, or the vote put for the election of the Member, or Commissioner for the said Shire, one of the Freeholders present entered a caveat, or protest, Rating and repeating the objections to the said Captain Charles Elphinstone Fleeming's(landing on the roll, or being admitted to vote as a Freeholder in the election of the Member, or Representative, for the said County; and further dating and objecting, that the said Captain Charles Elphinstone Fleeming was, by Law, incapable to be elected to represent the said Shire in Parliament; and that all the votes which should be be given in his favour should be held to be null and void, and considered as thrown away, as * having been given in favour of a person who was by Law ineligible for the reasons before assigned; and that, notwithstanding the above objections against the Cud Captain Vo l. 59.

Charles Elphinstone Fleeming (landing on the roll, or being admitted to vote as a Freeholder, and against his being capable to be elected the Representative to serve the said County in Parliament, a number of the Freeholders present did vote for the said Charles Elphinftone Fleeming, and the other Freeholders present, having voted for the Petitioner, the said Charles Elphinftone Fleeming was declared to be elected, and has been returned as the Representative for the County of Stirling to serve in this present Parliament; and that the Petitioner is advised, and humbly conceives, that the proceedings of the aforesaid meeting of the Freeholders of the County of Stirling, held upon the 19th of July, 1802, were illegal and unconstitutional, first, by inrolling the said Charles Elphinftone Fleeming as a Freeholder of the said County of Stirling, and afterwards in electing him to be the Representative in Parliament for the said Shire; and that the Returning Officer did wrong, and acted unwarrantably and unconditionally, by returning him the said Charles Elphinftone Fleeming as the person duly and legally elected to serve in the present Parliament for the said County of Stirling; and the Petitioner humbly conceives, and contends, that he was the ly person who, at the meeting aforesaid, was duly and lawfully elected the Representative of the said County of Stirling to serve in this present Parliament, and that he ought to have been returned accordingly, agreeably to a protest, or requisition, made and entered in the minutes of the Meeting by several of the Freeholders who voted for him; and that the election and return of the said Charles Elphinstone Fleeming was procured and obtained by the means above stated, and by other illegal, unwarrantable, and unconstitutional means and proceedings, to the great prejudice and injury of tho Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises under their consideration, and to resolve and declare that the majority of the Freeholders of the said County oF Stirling, at the aforesaid meeting held on the 19th of July 1802, did wrong, first by inrolling the said Charles Elphinstone Fleeming as a Freeholder of the said County of Stirling, and afterwards in electing him to be the Representative in this present Parliament for the said County of Stirling, and that the Returning Officer did wrong, and acted illegally and unconftitutionally, in returning him the said Charles Elphinftone Fleeming as the Representative duly elected for the said County of Stirling in the present Parliament; and to resolve and declare that, at the aforesaid meeting, the Petitioner was the only person who was duly and legally elected the Member or Representative to serve in this present Parliament for the said County of Stirling, and ought to have been returned accordingly; and to give the Petitioner such other and further relief or redrefe as to the House may seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into consideration upon Thursday the 1 ft day of March next, at three of the clock in the Afternoon.

Sir Francis Burdett reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants and Householders of the Parish of Saint Pancras, in the County of Middlesex, assembled in Vestry, and of other Inhabitant Householders, whose names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwardsdelivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. James Moore, Vestry Clerk, being examined, said,

' XI

That the said Parish is very large and populous, and the Poor belonging thereto are very numerous, inlomuch that the providing for the ("aid Poor, and the management and employment thereof, are become too burdcnlome for the Office of Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, which would be better discharged with the assistance of others participating in the powers and functions of the said Office, and forming, together with the said Overseers for the time being, one united and select body of Directors, for the governing, maintaining, and employing the said Poor, under proper rules and regulations to be established—That the present Workhouse of the said Parish is in many parts decayed, and with the buildings erected in addition thereto, is in all respects insufficient for the accommodation and proper employment of the Poor of the said Parish requiring to be supported therein; and, that it would tend to the better relief and accommodation of the said Poor, if a convenient building for their reception and'employment were provided by erecting a new Workhouse, either where the present Workhouse stands, with an enlargement of that lcite of ground by the purchase of additional grounds adjoining thereto, or in some other convenient situatioa within the said Parish, by the purchase of other grounds or buildings which may appear suitable to the above purposes.—And the witness added, That it would tend to render more productive the Poor Rates or AfilUinents of the said Parish, if powers were given to appoint Collectors of the said Rates 01 Assessments, with an allowance for their trouble in collecting the fame.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for providing in the Parish of Saint Pancras, in the County of Middlesex, a certain number of Directors, participating in the powers and functions of the Office of Overseers of the Poor, and forming, together with them and the Churchwardens and Vicar of the said Parish for the time being, one united and select body, for the better and more easy governing, maintaining, and employing the said Poor; for erecting a new Workhouse for the use of the said Parish, or purchasing ground or buildings suitable to that purpose, and providing for the expence of such purchase, and of such new building; and for rendering more productive the collection of the Poor Rates in the said Parish; and for other purposes: And that Sir Francis Burdett and Mr. Byng do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Francis William Grant, Esquire, being in his place, and having informed the House, That he was extremely concerned that the House should have had so much trouble on account of his absence from the Committee on the Waterford Election, which had arisen entirely from mifin-formation; that he wrote on the 5th of November to a Friend in town, to know whether the Committee was dif-lolved, wishing, at such a time as the present, to remain With his Regiment; but added, that it was his intention to set out from Dundee about the 17th of November, if his attendance was necessary: that the answer he received from his Friend was, that he conceived all Committees were dissolved by the prorogation of Parliament, but that he would make enquiry, and, if he found it otherwise, would give him information: that his Friend did not write to him again, and therefore he concluded the first information was right; and, that immediately on receiving the Order of the House, he set out for Londonhe also declared, that he had no intention to neglect or elude his duty, and, if he had known that his attendance was re-quisite, he certainly would not have exposed himself to the displeasure of the House; and he most humbly hoped that the House would be satisfied with this explanation and eicufe;

A Message from the Lords, by Sir William Weller Pepys and Mr. Pvpkam:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty the sum of eight thousand Pounds, for the present relief of certain Curates in England; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue, until six weeks after the commencement of the next Session of Parliament, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to empower the " Lord Lieutenant, or other Chief Governor or Governors " of Ireland, to apprehend and detain such Persons as he

" or they shall susped, for conspiring against His Majesty’s " Person and Government, until six weeks after the com-" mencement of the next Session of Parliamentwithout any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue, until six weeks after the commencement of the next Session of Parliament, an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for the suppref-" lion of Rebellion in Ireland, and for the protection of the " persons and property of His Majesty’s faithful Subjects " there, to continue in force until six weeks after the com-" mencement of the next Session of Parliamentwithout any Amendment: And also,

"The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue until the twenty-fifth day of March one thousand eight hundred and five, an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for discontinuing certain Drawbacks and Bounties on the Exportation of Sugar from Great Britain, and for allowing other Drawbacks and Bounties in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enabling the Lord Lieutenant, or other Chief Governor or Governors of Ireland, to prohibit, until the twenty-fifth day of March one thousand eight hundred and five, the Distillation of Spirits from Oats or Oatmeal in and for indemnifying such Persons as have acted in advising or carrying into execution a Proclamation of the Lord Lieutenant and Council of Ireland, for prohibiting such Distillation; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue several Laws relating to the suspending the operation of two Acts, of the fifteenth and seventeenth years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for restraining the Negotiation of Promissory Notes and Bills of Exchange, under a limited sum, in England and to the prohibiting the Exportation from, and permitting the Importation to. Great Britain, of Corn, and for allowing the Importation of other articles of provision, without Payment of Duty, until the twenty-fifth day of March one thousand eight hundred and five; and to the regulating the Trade and Commerce to and from the Isle of Malta, until six months after the Ratification of a Definitive Treaty of Peace} without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue, until the twenty-fifth day of March one thousand eight hundred and five, so much of an Act, made in the forty-first year of His present Majesty’s Reign, as relates to th.e prohibiting the Exportation from Ireland of Corn, or Potatoes, or other Provisions, and to the permitting the Importation into Ireland of Corn, Fish, and Provisions, without payment of Duty; without any Amendment; And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend two Acts,passed in the forty-first and forty-third years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for permitting Portugal Wine to be landed and warehoused in the United Kingdom, and to allow Spanish Wine to be so landed and warehoused; without any Amendment.

and in the fame line, leave out from " Corps" to " Provided" in line 9.

A Petition of Samuel Mitchell, JoJiak Abraham, William Petitions Walli/h, and several other Persons, whose names are there-unto subscribed, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Eicaion for setting forth, That at the last Election for Burgesses to Ij&eard. serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lijkeard in the County of Cornwall, held on or about the 6th July 1802, the Honourable John Eliot, the Honourable William Eliot, Thomas Sheridan, and William Ogilvie, Esquires, were Candidates; and that the Mayor, who acted as Returning Officer, returned the said Honourable John Eliot, and the said Honourable William Eliot, as duly elected to serve in Parliament as Burgesses for the said Borough of against which return two Petitions were presented to the House, one on behalf of the said Thomas Sheridan, Esquire, and William Ogilvie, Esquire, and one on behalf of Samuel.

Mitchell, Josiah Abraham, William Walli/h, and the several other Perfbhs whose names were thereunto subscribed. Inhabitants Householders of the said Borough of Lijkeard, paying, or liable to pay, Scotland Lot; stating, amongst other things, that the said Thomas Sheridan and William Ogilvie ought to have been duly elected to serve as Burgesses in Parliament for the said Borough, they having a majority of legal votes; and that on Fiiday the 25th day of February last, a Select Committee of the House was appointed to try the merits of the said Petitions; and that the said Committee, on the hearing of the said Petitions, required the parties to deliver in separate statements of the several rights of election for the said Borough for which they respectively contended; and- that the state-rnent delivered in by the Petitioners to Parliament before the said Committee, dated the right of election in the said Borough of Lijkeard to be in the Inhabitants paying, or liable to pay, Scotland Lot; and that the statement delivered in by the fitting Members dated the right of election to be in the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough of Lijkeard-, and that the said Committee, after having heard the evidence adduced by the said several Parties in proof of the right of election so dated to the said Committee as aforesaid, determined that the right of election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Lijkeard was not in the Inhabitants paying, or liable to pay, Scotland Lot; the said Committee also determined, that the right of election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Lif-keard was in the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough; and the said Resolutions were accordingly reported by the said Select Committee to the House: The Petitioners therefore, being advised that the said Resolutions and Determination of the said Select Committee of the House, on the said right of election, is contrary to Law, pray that they may be admitted as Parties to oppose that right of election which has been deemed valid, in the judgment of the said Committee, as aforesaid, and to support and establish the said right of election for which they contended before the said Select Committee, and which was negatived by the said Select Committee of the House, or such other right as shall be confident with Law; and that such relief may be granted them as the justice of the case may require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into consideration upon Tuesday, the ioth day of April next, at Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Robert Harrison, who has been Clerk to the Petitioners up-

wards of 17 years, being examined, said, That the Petitioners have, at a very great expence, promoted and encou-*. raged the arts of Painting and Engraving, which for several years pall has given great encouragement to the Art ills therein, and greatly contributed to the securing to this Country, a pre-eminence over all other nations in. those arts: That in the course of this pursuit, besides various other large works published in a moll splendid manner, the Plays of Shakspeare, ornamented with Engravings from Pictures by English Artiffcs, and for which pictures, and the exhibiting the fame with their other works, the Petitioners erected a building in Pall Mall, called The Shakspeare Gallery at a very confiaerable expence, and in com* pleting that establishment, in addition to their former and other works, have so extended their concerns, and increased the size, value, and expence of their Collection of Paintings,

Drawings, and Engravings, as to make them much too great a concern for them to retain.—And being further examined, the Witness said. That the Collection cannot be difoofed of by the common way of fele, but at a very great lols to the Petitioners; and that, unless some encouragement, under the fenftion of Parliament, be given to them, to enable them to dispose of their said Collection to the best advantage, their endeavours to serve the Public, will prove highly detrimental to themselves.

A Petition of the Land Owners, Barley Growers, and Petitions of Maltsters, of the County of Norfolk: And also. Barley Grow-

A Petition of the Land Owners, Barley Growers, and KorMk^nd Maltsters, of the County of Suffolk,' whole names arc Suffolk, thereunto subscribed;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have, with the utmost concern, seen that the late heavy additional Duties on Malt have occasioned a considerable decrease in the consumption of Barley; and that they admit that the Barley crop of 1801 was good and abundant, but, from causes unknown to them (till lately) the sale of Barley became all at once dull, and a gradual decrease in the price succeeded; and that the Petitioners conceive that the great and unexpected rapid decrease in the sale and price of Barley was owing to the rectifying Distillers of this part of the kingdom supplying themselves with Raw Spirits from Ireland considerably cheaper than the Malt# Distillers of this country could afford to supply them, in consequence of which the Malt Distillers did but little business during the season, and the Barley Gowers thereby sustained considerable loss by the decrease it occasioned in the consumption and price of their Barley, and the public a decrease in its Revenue; and that as no foreign market for Barley or Malt is likely to offer, the Petitioners are apprehensive the fame may become wholly unfaleable after the Brewers shall have taken off their usual consumption, unless a Drawback on the Exportation of Spirits is allowed the English Distillers, to induce them to consume it; and that the Petitioners also conceive that, in consequence of the Union with Ireland, and the great change the Corn Trade of Europe has undergone within the last ten years, the Corn Act of the 31st of His present Majesty is wholly inadequate to the purpose intended by the Legislature at that time, extremely unequal in its operation, injurious to agriculture, and requires to be revised and altered according to existing circumstances: And therefore praying, That the House will take the above matters into its early consideration, that the revenue Laws respecting the importing VValh or Raw Spirits from Scotland and Ireland may be

That, for want of a good Harbour in Carnarvon Bay, on the Coast of the District of Llun, in the County of Carnarvon, a great number of vessels have been from time to time, shipwrecked, the lives of many brave Seamen have been loft, and the trade carried on through St. George's Channel has been thereby materially injured, and is exposed to great risque and peril; and that a good Harbour in the said Bay, on the Coast of the said District of Lldn, would not only prevent the occurrence of similar misfortunes, and afford shelter and security to Vessels trading through the said Channel, but would also facilitate the communication between Great Britain and Ireland; and that, if a Pier, and other Works, were erected in the Harbour of Porthdinllain,in the said Bay, and on the

Coast of the said District, it would be an excellent Harbour, capable of affording complete protection to the largest Vessels trading through the said Channel, and would, from its favourable situation, and other circumstances, open the most direct, expeditious, and secure communication between London and "Dublin: And therefore praying. To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, two Acts jpafied in the'33d year of his late Majesty, and in the zzd

year of His present Majesty, for laying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or one-sixth part of a Penny sterling on every Scots pint of Ale, Porter, or Beer, brewed lor sale, or vended in the said Town and Parish, to be applied fur repairing the Streets, and supplying the Inhabitants with Water, were read: And,

Sir William Geary reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several persons, whole names are thereunto subscribed, being interested in the trade, commerce, navigation, and prosperity of this Kingdom, was referred; That the Committee had examined the mat ter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas King, Assistant Secretary to The Marine Society, being examined, said, That the extension and improvement of Fisheries are of the highest importance to the preservation of the wealth, trade, commerce, navigation, and naval strength of this Kingdom; and that the establishment of a Fishing Company, would tend to the general prosperity of the Country, and advance the objects of the Institution of The Marine Society, by finding employment for great numbers of industrious Poor, and by training up for the Navy multitudes of destitute and friendless Boys, and would also be the means of reducing the price of provisions by an increase of wholesome food; and that the establishment of such a Company in the Metropolis, on account of its great and increasing population, would likewise be productive of very extensive advantages.— And being further examined, he said. That a plan for ac-complishing this desirable object, has been maturely considered and agreed upon, and Subscriptions to a considerable amount entered into for that purpose.—Then,

Mr. Thomas Howell being examined, confirmed the foregoing evidence.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill, for incorporating certain . persons, and their l'uccelTors, by the name of The Marine Society Fishing Company, for increasing the supply of Fish, for advancing the objects of the institution of The Marine Society, and for conducting and supporting the establishment of such Company: And that Sir William Geary and Mr. Blackburn of Newport do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That owing to the extension of the said City, and great increase of the Inhabitants therein, the Suburbs thereof, and places adjacent, it has become necessary to have a general system of Police established for the City, Canongate and Pleasance, and all other places within the present Toll Bars erected on the respective High Roads leading to the said City, and the Houses adjacent thereto; and also for North Leith and Citadel, and the Villages of New-haven, Bonington, Canonmilns, Water of Leith, Rejlalrig, Jocks Lodge, and Portobello, and to have a permanent Magistrate or Justice of the Peace to superintend the whole, with proper powers, and to have Deputies where necessary; and that it has likewise become necessary to have regulations for cleaning and lighting the streets and passages within the aforesaid places; and that a proper number of Watchmen, both by night and day, Be appointed; and also regulations made for the apprehending and punishing of vagrants and disorderly persons who cannot give a proper account of themselves; and also for the more effectual sup-pression of common begging, and removing all kinds of nuisances from the streets and roads within the above limits, and for other purposes tending to the preservation of peace and good order within the City and Suburbs; and that a Tax be imposed upon the whole Inhabitants within the aforesaid limits, for defraying the expence, under the administration of Commissioners; and that it is necessary to veil the Petitioners, the Lord Provost and Magistrates, with more ample powers for licensing and making, and enforcing Regulations and Fares for Hackney Coaches, Chairs, Carts, Porters, Meters of Corns, as well for Edinburgh as in their Port of Leith; and that the Inhabitants have been very much imposed upon in the weight of coals brought in carts to the City and adjacent places, and it will therefore be necessary to authorize the Lord Provost and Magistrates to appoint every Cart to be weighed at Still-yards, to be created for the purpose; and to exact for each Cart a small sum of money sufficient for the payment of persons for fu-perintending the weighing and keeping in repair the Still-yards, the money to be repaid to the drivers of Carts by the conlumers and purchalerS of the Coals, and to make and enforce regulations for that purpose; and that it is necessary to authorize the Lord Prcrvoft and Magistrates to Vol. 59.

take cognizance of Bread, and to make and enforce Regulations for making it of an uniform weight at whatever the felling price may be, whether baked in Edinburgh or in the Suburbs, or brought there from the Country; and that it is also necessary to extend the Royalty over certain grounds lately purchased by the City, and other grounds on the north of the City, belonging in property to the Governors of George Heriot's Hospital, and the Trustees of David Steuart, Esquire: And therefore praying. ing of an undue election and return for the County of the Town of Carrickfergus, being come;

The Serjeant at Arms was lent, with the Mace, to the places adjacent, to require the attendance of the Members on the business of the House.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and eighty-eight Members only being present,

Mr. Speaker directed the Clerk to read the Order of the day, for taking the said Petition into consideration; and immediately adjourned the fame till Tommorrow, at Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

The Order of the day being read, for taking into consideration the Petition, complaining of an undue election and return for the Borough of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk;

Ordered, That the consideration of the said Petition be adjourned till Tommorrow, at half an hour after Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

Resolved, That, when the House shall have proceeded, Tomorrow, to the appointment of Select Committees, for the trial of the several Petitions which are appointed to be then taken into consideration, and the names of the Members shall be drawn, and called for that purpose, Mr. Speaker do direct the name of every Member so called, who shall be absent from the House, and who shall not then be serving on Select Committees for trial of controverted elections, to be let aside: And that a list of the names of such absent Members be reported, by Mr. Speaker, to the House, at such time as the House shall think fit to appoint.

Resolved, That, upon the Report of the lift of the names of such absent Members, the Members, for whose non-attendance on the appointment of the said several Select Committees, asufficient excuse shall not be made, and allowed by the House, shall be forthwith ordered to be taken into the custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, and shall not be discharged out of custody, without the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicenle, That this House be called over Tommorrow.

Ordered, That such Members as shall not then attend, be fefit for in custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

And then the House was adjourned till Tommorrow Morning, Ten of the clock.

A Petition of several Journeymen Calico Printers, and Calico others working in that trade, in the Counties of Lancaster, £nntfr$ Derby, Chester, and Stafford, in England, and in the Coun- ctul'/n' ties of Lanark, Renfrew, Dunbarton, Stirling, and in

Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That great numbers of the Petitioners, and other Journeymen Calico Printers, have, for aferics of years past, been greatly distressed for want of work in their trade, and that this distress has chiefly arisen from a very general, if hot universal, practice of the Mailer Calico Printers in the Counties above enumerated, who (yftematically carry on the said trade by employing in it, in many instances, a greater number of Out-door Apprentices than of Journeymen, and, upon an average, nearly two of such Apprentices to three Journeymen, a practice of great injury to the Petitioners, their families, and, ultimately, even to the Apprentices themselves; and that one of the injurious effects to the Petitioners by this system is, that, in many in (lances, Boys are taken as Apprentices to the said trade or business on verbal agreement, whereby they are at liberty to absent themselves from the service and controul ot their Mailers on any trifling disagreement, and are generally replaced by others, thereby creating an overstock of hands in the said trade: And therefore praying. That leave may be given to bring in a Bill to regulate the trade or business of Calico Printers.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the same, as it dial I appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Blackburne of Lancafiire, Mr.

Stanley, &c.: And they are to meet Tommorrow Morning, at Nine of the clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for persons, papers, and records.

A Petition of several Justices of the Peace acting in and for the County of Leicester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at the Castle of Leicester, on the 19th day of April last, it appeared to the Court, that the AssefTment, by which the County Rates are collected, had not been altered since 1740, and is becoming very unequal, from the great alterations which have taken place in the value of property in that long period of time; and that there are thirty Lordships, or Places, in the said County; which are not rated in the general County Rate, made under the powers of the Act of the 12th of George the Second, or have been since discharged from that Rate because the powers of the said Act are inadequate to in-force the payment thereof; and that the injury of this unequal taxation, to many parts of the said County, is further aggravated by, the great increase of the County-Expenditure, which, in the last thirty years, hath advanced from £.560. to about £.3,00®. per annum-, and it is become expedient that a more equal and effectual method of making the County Rates, within the said County; should be established: And therefore praying. That leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Barley Growers, Maltsters, Consumers of Malt, and Landholders in general, of the Counties of Stafford and Warwick, was pretented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Taxes on Malt are extremely oppressive, and particularly objectionable in those Counties where the common beverage is Beer, and fall with peculiar force on the Petitioners; and that all Bounties on the Importation of Corn are extremely prejudicial to this Country, and ought not to be fullered but in cases of the greatest emergency: And therefore praying the House to take the above matters into its early consideration, and that the Corn Act, of the 31ft year of His present Majesty, may be revised and amended.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John RobinJ'on being examined, said. That the Fisheries in the said arm of the Sea, and in the several Rivers, Rivulets, Brooks, Streams, Ponds, Pools, and other Waters wlvch run into, and otherwise communicate with, the said arm of the Sea, were formerly of great value to the Owners, Occupiers, and Farmers thereof, and of much public utility; but, from the great destruction which hath of late years been made therein by persons of all descriptions destroying the Breeding Kepper and Shedder Salmon, and other Fish, and the Brood, Spawn, and Fry thereof, which are bred in the said arm of the Sea, and other Waters which run into, or communicate therewith, the said Fisheries have fallen into great decay, and become nearly useless and unprofitable, to the great loss of the Public, as well as to the individuals interested therein: That if proper Rules were established for the better protecting and preserving the Breeding Salmon and other fish and the Brood, Spawn, and Fry thereof in the said Fisheries, and for ascertaining the times when the different forts of fish shall be taken and killed, it would not only be the means of their prefeivation, but also tend to the improvement of the estates and properties of the Petitioners, and all others concerned therein, and likewise be of public utility.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for better regulating and improving the Fisheries in the arm of the Sea between the County of Cumberland and the Counties of Dumfries and W, and the Stewartry of Kirkcudbright, and also the Fisheries in the several Streams and Waters which run into, or communicate with, the said arm of the Sea: And that Lord Viscount Stopford and Mr. Cunven do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Legh Keck reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Justices of the Peace acting in and for the County of Leicester,was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

* Thomas Frere being examined, laid. That at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace holden at the Castle of Leicester,in the said County, on the 19th day of April

lad, it appeared to the Court, that the Assessment by which the County Rates are collected, had not been altered since the year 1740, and is becoming very unequal, from the great alterations which have taken place in the value of property in that long period of time: That there are 30 Lordships or Places in the said County, which are not rated in the General County Rate made under the powers of the Act of the 12th of George the Second, or have been since discharged from that Rate, because the powers of the said last mentioned Act were inadequate to enforce the payment thereof: That the injury of this unequal taxation, to many parts of the said County, is further aggravated by the great encrease of the County expenditure, which in the lad 30 years hath advanced from £.560. to about £.3,000. per annum, and it is therefore become expedient that a more equal and effectual method of making the County Rates, within the said County, should be established.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for empowering the Justices of the Peace for the County of Leicester, at their General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, to make a fair and equal County Rate for the said County: And that Mr. Legh Keck and Sir Edmund do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several free Fishermen of the Fisheries of Faversham, Milton, Whit ft able, and in the County of Kent, being the Foremen and principal Officers representing the said Fisheries, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for incorporating certain persons, and their successors, by the name of The Marine Society Fishing Company, for increasing the supply of

Fish, for advancing the objects of the institution of The Marine Society, and for conducting and supporting the establishment of such Company; and letting forth. That the said Fisheries raise a very large proportion of Seamen, and that several hundred persons are altogether dependent thereon for the support of themselves and families; and that the Petitioners are apprehend ve, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it may materially prejudice the said Fisheries, and deprive the Petitioners, and those dependent on them, of the means of getting their living: And therefore praying. A Petition of the Trustees of The British Museum, being offered to be prefen ted to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty’s command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That in the 2d year of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the sum allowed them for the establishment and support of the said Museum was reduced to a capital of £.30,000. Reduced Bank Annuities, the dividend of which, amounting to £.900. was, notwithstanding their utmo'ft attention to the forming their establishment with frugality, greatly infus-ficient for that purpose,' upon which re pre fen tat ion they have at sundry times obtained from the House various sums to supply the deficiency of their income; which sums, together with the salary allotted to the King’s Librarian, yearly amounting to about £.250. have proved infuificient to defray the necessary expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the hands of the Trustees is not sufficient to carry on the purposes of the trust, without the aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to grant them such farther support towards enabling them to carry on the execution of the trust reposed in them by Parliament, for the general benefit of learning and -useful knowledge, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of the several Sums that have been already granted for the service of The British Museum, and of the Expenditure thereof.

Mr. Nicholas Vansittart reported from the Committee appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near ex-Voj.. 59.

piring, and to report their Opinion, from time to time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; That the Committee had made a fur: ther Enquiry, and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 41ft year of His present Majesty, as relates to allowing Plantation

Sugar to be warehoused, which has been continued by several subsequent Acts until the 25th day of March 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued and amended:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 35th year of His present Majesty, for allowing the Importation of Rape Seed, and other Seeds uled for extracting Oil, which has been amended and continued by several subsequent Acts until the 24th day of June 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued and amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 31ft year of His present Majesty, to allow the Importation of Seal Skins, cured with foreign salt, free of Duty, which has been continued by several subsequent Acts until the 24th day of June 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued and amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 41ft year of His present Majesty, as relates to allowing the use of Salt, Duty free, in the preserving of Fish in bulk, or in barrels; and to discontinuing the Bounty payable on white Herrings exported, which has been continued by several subsequent Acts until the 25th day of March 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 39th year of His present Majesty, to continue and amend so much of an Act, made in the 33d year of His laid Majesty, as permits Sir William , George Bishop, and Argles Bishop, to carry on the manufacture of Maidstone Geneva; which Act was to continue in force for five years, from the 5th day of July 1799, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, to repeal the Duties of Customs payable in Great Britain, and to grant other Duties in lieu thereof, as relates to the admission to entry of Oil, or Blubber, of Fish or creatures living in the sea, actually caught and taken on the Banks and Shores of the Island of Newfoundland, and parts adjacent, wholly by His Majesty’s subjects carrying on the said Fishery from His Majesty’s European dominions, and usually residing in the said dominions, on payment of the Duty by the said Act imposed on Train Oil or Blubber of Newfoundland, of British Fishing, which was to continue in force until the 25th day of December 1804, is near ex-, piring, and fit to be continued.

jRe,/o/im/, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 26th year of His present Majesty, for the further support and encouragement of the Fisheries carried on in the Greenland Seas and Davis's,

which was to be in force for five years, from the 25th day of December 1786; and also so much of an Act, made in the 29th year of His said Majesty, as relates to the Fisheries carried on in the Greenland Seas and Davis's Streights, which were, by several subsequent Acts, amended and further continued until the 25th day of December 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued, except so much thereof as relates to allowing Vefl'ds employed in the said Fisheries to complete the number of men at certain Ports.

reported. That you, upon your examination as a Witness, were guilty of gross and, wilful prevarication.

In the corrupt and scandalous scenes which disgraced that election, it appears that you have borne a considerable part; by you the electors were invited to- bring about a plan for general bribery; by your means that plan was matured and executed; and the freedom of election, and the privileges of this House, have been violated for a time with success and impunity.

But such triumphs never have been, or can be, of long continuance. The confusion and embarrassment of a guilty conscience bave,in your subsequent conduct,plunged you into further guilt; and you have been the first to suffer by the consequences of those criminal, practices in which you were the foremost to involve others.

Upon the Report from the Committee, that you had prevaricated in giving your evidence, the House thought fit to mark its heavy displeasure by imprisoning you in the Common Gaol of Newgate, and stigmatizing you, as an example to deter others; but it now deems its justice to be satisfied so far as relates to that offence, the rest of your misconduct being reserved for future consideration: And the House having ordered that you be now discharged out of custody, you are discharged accordingly, paying your fees.

A Petition of several Owners and Occupiers of Mills and Manufactories on the Rivers Wandle, Ewell, Mole, and RavenJborne, in the Counties of Surrey and Kent, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, from the Croydon Canal, at or near the Town of Croydon, in the County of Surrey, into the River Arun, at or near Arundel, in the County of Sussex; and from the said River to, and to communicate with, the Harbour of ,in the County of Southampton; and setting forth. That if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it would be extremely prejudicial and ruinous to the several persons having property, and occupying Mills and Manufactories on the above Rivers: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, counsel, agents, and witnesses, against the said Bill j and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of several Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Houses in the vicinity of the proposed Canal from Croydon to Portsmouth,was also presented to the House, and

read; likewise taking notice of the said Bill; and setting forth. That the said intended Canal, with its Reservoirs, will consume above 2,000 acres of land, and that much valuable property belonging to the Petitioners will be destroyed, or very materially injured, in the trial of such project, even G ugh it should be afterwards abandoned, and which, if eventually executed, will be attended with the most serious consequences to the property of Individuals, without offering any public advantages to compenfete the mischiefs it will :nevitably occasion; and that the project is undertaken qn a> very inadequate subscription of persons, a very few indeed of whom are at all connected with the Counties through which the Canal is intended to pass: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves, their counsel, agents, and witnesses, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a second time j and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, their counsel, agents, and witnesses, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a second time To-

Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to considerof the Acts mentioned in the Ilefolutions which, upon Tuesday last, were reported from the Committee appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion, from time to time, so the House, which of them are fit to be revived, continued, of made perpetual, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame were read; and are as followeth; viz

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 41ft year of His present Majesty, as relates to allowing British Plantation Sugar to be warehoused, which has been continued by several subse-quest-Acts until the 15th day of March 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued and amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 35th year of His present Majesty, for allowing the Importation of Rape Seed, and other Seeds used for extracting Oil, which has been amended and continued by leyeral subsequent Acts until the 24th day of June 1804, is near expiring, and lit to be continued and amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 31ft year of His present Majesty, to allow the Importation of Seal Skins, cured with Foreign Salt, free of Duty, which has been continued by several subsequent Acts until the 24th day of June 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued and amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That lb much of an Act, made in the 41ft year of His present Majesty, as relates to allowing the use of Salt, Duty free, in the preserving of Fish in bulk, or in barrels, and to discontinuing the Bounty payable on White Herrings exported, which has been continued by several subsequent Acts-until the 25th day of March 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 39th year of His present Majesty, to continue and amend so much of an Act, made in the 33d year of His liud Majesty, as permits Sir William Bijhcp, George Bijhp, and Angles Bishop, to carry on the manufacture of Matd/lone Geneva; which Act was to continue in

force for five years, from the 5th day of July 1799, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That It is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament,

to repeal the Duties of Customs payable in Great Britain, and to grant other Duties in lieu thereof, as relates to the admission to entry of Oil, or Blubber, of Fish or Creatures living in the Sea, actually caught and taken on the Banks and Shores of the Island of Newfoundland, and parts adjacent, wholly by His Majesty’s Subjects carrying on the said Fishery from His Majesty’s European dominions, and usually redding in the said dominions, on payment of the Duty by the said Act imnofed on Train Oil or Blubber of Newfoundland, o( British Fishing, which was to continue in force until the 2;th day of December 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Ri fo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 26th year of His present Majesty, for the further support and encouragement of the Fisheries carried on in the Greenland Seas and Davis's Straights, which was to be in force for five years, from the 25th day of December 17S6; and a!!o so much of an Act, made in the 29th year of His find Majesty, as relates to the Fisheries carried on in the Greenland Seas and Davis's Streights, which were,by several subsequent Acts,amended and further continued until the 25th day of December 1804, is near expiring, and fit to be continued, except so much thereof as relates to allowing VefieL employed in the said Fisheries to complete the number of men at certain Ports.
