A Petition of William Hujkijfcn, of Eartliam, in the B

County of Sussex, Esquire, was presented to the House, and

read; letting forth. That at the last Election of a Burgess Lifce^rd to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Elct*,on-UJkeard, in the County of Cornwall, held on the 9th day of March instant, 'Thomas Sheridan, Esquire, and the Peti- 1

tioner, were Candidates; and that by the last decilion of a 1

Committee of the House, on the 9th day of March 1803, the right of election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament '•

for the said Borough of Lijkeard was declared to be in the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough, and was accordingly so reported to the House; and that the Mayor of the;

said Borough for the time being is the Returning Officer, and that no other person hath ever exercised, or claimed to exercise, that right; and that the Under Sheriff of the County of Cornwalltransmitted the Precept for the election of a Burgess, in pursuance of a Writ for that purpose, on the 4th day of March instant, by his own messenger, to Edmund Carthew, Esquire, the present Mayor of tire laid

Borough, which precept was directed to, and delivered to,

the Mayor of the said Borough of Lijkeard, as such Returning Officer; and that the said Edmund Carthew, as such Mayor, made the necessary Proclamation for the said election taking place on the 9th day of March instant, and which accordingly came on upon that day; and that the said Mayor, and twenty other Burgesses of the said Borough, voted for the Petitioner, and three Burgesses only for the said Thomas Sheridan; and that the Petitioner was thereupon declared by the said Mayor duly elected, and an Indenture of Return of the Petitioner, bearing date on the said 9th day of March, was duly executed by the said Mayor, under the common seal of the said Borough, and by nineteen of the said twenty Burgesses, whole names and seals are also thereunto affixed; and that on the 10th day of March instant, such Indenture, annexed to the said Precept, was transmitted to Mr. John Dayman, the Under Sheriff of Thomas Rawlings, Esquire, Sheriff of the said County, by the said Mayor, and who thereupon executed the counterpart in the name of the said Sheriff, and exchanged the fame with the said Mayor; and that the return of the said Mayor, on the back of the Precept, was of one Indenture only, by which the Petitioner was returned as a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, and such Indenture only was annexed thereto; and that, notwithstanding such return of the said Mayor, as Returning Officer for the said Borough, to the said Sheriff, as will appear by the Precept filed with the said Writ and Return, the said Sheriff, contrary to his duty, and wilfully and corruptly to deprive the Petitioner of repre-fenting the said Borough in Parliament, as he lawfully ought, hath annexed, in his return to the said Writ, without the privity of the said Mayor, a second schedule, purporting to be an Indenture made between the said Mayor and Burgesses of the one part, and the said Sheriff of the other part, by which the said Thomas Sheridan is returned as duly elected for the said Borough of Lijkeard (a copy of which Indenture is annexed to the said Petition); and that it appears, upon the face of such Indenture (and as the fad; is) that it neither has the (ignature, or seal, of the said Mayor; and that, by such gross and comipt conduct of the said Under Sheriff, the Petitioner, though duly elected, is prevented from taking his feat for the said Borough of Lijkeard: And therefore praying, That the House will grant such relief in the preniifes as the nature of the case may require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend Deputy clerk, this House, Tommorrow, with the last return of a Member ^attend0"* to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Lijkeard, in the County of Cornwall.

A Petition of the Land Owners, Land Occupiers, and Maltsters, of the County of was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, That the present operation of the Corn Laws, combined with certain other causes, to which the Petitioners intreat the attention of the House, is likely to affect materially the agriculture of the Kingdom, and has already occasioned to the Petitioners very considerable injury; and that the provisions of the last Corn Act, of the 31st of His Majesty’s Reign, are wholly unsuited to the present times; and that the late very heavy additional Duties on Malt and Beer have, in a great mea-l'ure, decreased the consumption of Barley, and thereby materially contributed to the extreme reduction of the price thereof: And therefore praying. Mr. Hiley Addington reported from the Committee, appointed to consider of the mod speedy and effectual mode of adjusting such differences as may arise between Masters and Workmen engaged in the Cotton Manufacture, and to report the fame, as it should appear to them, to the House; and to whom the Minutes of the Evidence taken before the Committee on the Petitions, presented to the House in the last Session of Parliament, and also the several proceedings of the House, or of any Committee thereof, in the same Session, relating to the Cotton Manufacture, were severally referred; and who were instrufted to consider of proper mealiires to be taken for preventing such differences, and to report the several matters referred to them, together with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with several Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read 'the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee having perused and considered the Minutes of the Evidence taken before the Committee, to whom the several Petitions, presented to the House in the last Session of Parliament, relating to the Act of the 39th and 40th year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for settling disputes that may arise between Masters and " Workmen engaged in the Cotton Manufacture in that " part of Great Britain called ,"were referred j and

having taking into their consideration the Bill for amending the said Act, which was presented to the House in the last Session of Parliament, for the more effectually settling such disputes, have come to the following Resolutiofts:

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Act of the 39th and 4.0th year of His present Majesty, for settling disputes between Masters and Workmen engaged in the Cotton Manufacture in England, has not produced the good effects that were expected from it.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the principle and object of the said Act was the establishment ofa ftiort, summary, impartial, and competent Tribunal, for the determination of all disputes arising between Masters and Workmen engaged in the said Manufacture, respecting. the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the power given by the said Act to Masters and Workmen respectively to nominate persons to hear and determine disputes arising between them, respecting the said Manufacture, has been productive of great inconveniences and delay.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that so much of the said Act, of the 39th and 40th year of His present Majesty, as empowers the Masters and Workmen, in case of such disputes, respectively to nominate persons to hear and determine such disputes, should be repealed, and that in lieu thereof, it should be provided, that in cases of disputes between Masters and Workmen engaged in the said Manufacture respecting such Manufacture, any Justice of the Peace for the County, Town, Division, or Place, wherein such dispute may arise, shall be empowered and required to hear, and finally determine, such dispute, if the parties to such dispute shall, by writing, under their hands, so require; and if they (halt not so require, then that such Justice shall forthwith nominate four impartial persons, residing in or near to the place where such dispute shall have arilen, two of whom shall be Masters, or Agents or Foremen of Masters, and the other two Workmen, from and out of which persons so nominated

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee (although they are aware of the caution which is requisite in the application of Legislative Regulations to internal arrangements in the concerns of Trade or Manufacture) That it is expedient, in the present circumstances, with a view to prevent, as far as may be possible, any disputes arising between Matters and Workmen engaged in the above Manufacture, to provide, that with every piece of work hereafter to be delivered out by, or on behalf of, any Matter to any Workman engaged therein, there shall be given, by the person delivering out the same to such Workman, if required by such Workman, a Ticket, signed by the person delivering out the fame, dating the quantity of the materials delivered out, the nature of the work to be done, and the price or terms agreed upon for the executing such work in a workmanlike manner.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the expences which may be incurred in the determination of such disputes, should be limited by (ome specific Regulations.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further con-(ideration upon Monday, the 9th day of April next.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed for the Members of the House.

Ordered, That there be lajd before this House, an Account of the Amount of Duties received within the Ports of the Isle of Man upon Imports and Exports, between the iftof January 1798 and the ift of January 1804, distinguishing the Amount of each year; together with an Account of all Sums paid out of the Duties so received for Salaries, Bounties, Buildings, or otherwise; together with the Amount of Balance of Surplus Revenue up to the ift of January 1798.

That by the Statute Law of Scotland, all Cruives,

.Zaires, and Fish Dams, within salt water, where the tide ebbs and flows, are ordained to be utterly destroyed and put down, and all Cruives and Zaires that are let upon sands and (hoals far within the water, be destroyed and put away for ever, excepting the Cruives and Zaires being upon the Water of Solzuay, which, at the time of making the aforesaid Laws, was the March between the two independent Kingdoms of England and Scotland; and that the said Fisheries were formerly of great value to the Owners and Occupiers of the fame, and of much public utility, but have become gradually less productive by the erection of Cruives, Zaires, Fish Yards, Chamber Nets, and other engines and devices formerly not practised or known in these parts; and also by the great destruction of breeding Salmon, Kepper, and Sheddar Salmon, Gilfes,

•Trouts, and Whitings, otherwise Hidings, and of the Fry

• or young Brood thereof, whereby the said Fisheries have •been rendered and are become altogether unprofitable; and

nearly ufeiefs, to the great hurt and prejudice of the Public, as well as of the Individuals interested therein; and that ' owing to the great distance the Petitioners, and the several other persons interested in the said Fisheries, reside from each other, and the variety of information necessary to be collected respecting the erection of the engines and devices before-mentioned, and the best mode-of protecting the said Fisheries, the Petitioners, and the several other persons interested therein, were not enabled to present a Petition to the House, praying for leave to bring in a Bill to remedy the abuses aforesaid, until the time limited'by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills had elapsed; and that it will be a great inconvenience and prejudice to the Petitioners, as well as to the Public, if leave be not given

not intend to defend his return for the said Borough.

And the said Declaration being delivered in at the Table, was read; and is as followeth; viz.

" To the Right honourable The Speaker of the House " of Commons.

* I Thomas Sheridan, of George-street,

Esquire, having been returned by the Sheriff of Cornwall, a Member to serve in this present Parliament, for the Borough of Liskeard, in the said County of Cornwall, together with William Hujkijfon, Esquire, who has petition-

" George-street,

stated the right of election to be in the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Borough; and that the said Committee, after having heard the evidence adduced by the several parties in proof of the right of election so stated to the said Committee as aforesaid, determined that the right of election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough was not in the Inhabitants paying, or liable to pay, scot and lot; and the said Committee also determined, that the right of election for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough was in the Mayor and Burgesses; which Resolutions were accordingly reported by the said Select Committee to the House: And that the Petitioners being advised that such Resolutions and Determinations of the said Select Committee on the said right of election were contrary to Law, a Petition was presented by them and others, whose names are thereto subscribed, Rating the several matters and things hereinbefore dated; and praying, that they might be admitted as parties to oppose that right of election w'hich has been deemed valid in the judgment of the said Select Committee as aforesaid, and to support and establish that right of election for which they contended before the said Select Committee, and which was negatived by the said Select Committee, or such other right as might be confident with Law; and that such other relief might be granted to them as the justice of the case might require; which said last mentioned Petition is ordered to be taken into consideration by the House on the 17th day of April next, as by the Votes of the House will more fully appear; and that on the 9th day of this instant March, an election took place of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Lif-keard, in the room of the said John Eliot (now Lord Eliot) who had vacated his feat, being called up to the House of Lords on the death of his father, the late Lord at which election the said ‘Thomas Sheridan and Huf-

kijfon, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the Petitioners and others, claiming a right to vote at such election as Inhabitants of the said Borough, paying, or liable to pay, scot and lot, and conceiving that such right could not have been defeated by the decision of the said Select Committee, so petitioned against as aforesaid, duly tendered their votes to the Mayor (who acted as Returning Officer) for the said ’Thomas Sheridan at such election, which votes the said Mayor took upon himself, without lawful and sufficient cause, to disallow and rejeftj and that the said Mayor ought to have returned the said Thomas Sheridan duly elected to serve as a Burgess in Parliament for the said Borough, he having the majority of legal votes, notwithstanding which the fit id Mayor thought proper to return the said William HuJliJJ’on; and that the said Mayor admitted divers persons to vote for the said William HnJ-kijfon at the said last mentioned election, who were not entitled to vote at such election: And therefore praying, That in case the Petition of right, now pending before the House, be decided in favour of the Petitioners, and those claiming a right to vote as Inhabitants of the said Borough of Lijkeard,paying, or liable to pay, scot and lot, the election of the said William Hujkijfon may be declared null and void; and that the said Thomas Sheridan may be declared to have been duly elected; and that the return may be amended accordingly.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into consideration upon Monday, the 23d day of this inllant April, at the same time that the Petition of Thomas Esquire, which was presented to the House upon the 28th day of March lait, is ordered to be taken into consideration.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of several Acts made for regulating the trials of controverted elections or returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like.Notices, as in former cases, were sent to the parties, accom-

panied with Orders for their attendance, by them-lelves, their counsel or agents, at the time on which the said Petition is ordered to be taken into consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his warrant, of warrants, for such persons, papers, and records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several parties, on the hearing of the matter of the said Petition.

And then the House adjourned till Tommorrow Morning, Ten of the clock.

MR. fames Graham reported from (he Committee, to Solway-whom the Petition uf several Owners and Proprietors of Fisheries in the Water of Solway, otherwise called Sol- reported! way Frith, and in the I ivers of Eden, Ejhe, and Annan, communicating therewith, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as folluweth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. nathan Holmes being examined said. That by the Statute Law of Scotland all Cruives, Zaires, and Fish Dams, within salt water, where the tide ebbs and flows, are ordained to be utterly destroyed and put down, and all Cruives and Zferes, that are let upon lands and Ihoals far within the water, be destroyed and put away for ever, excepting the Cruives and Zaires being upon the water of Solway, which, at the time of making the aforesaid Laws, was the march between the two independent kingdoms of England and Scotland-, and that the said Fisheries,were formerly of great value to the Owners and Occupiers of the fame, and of much public utility, but have become gradually left productive by the erection of Cruives, Zaires,

Fish Yards, Chamber Nets, and other engines and devices, formerly not practised or known in these parts; and also by the great destruction cf breeding Salmon, Kepper, and Sheddar Salmon, Gilfes, Trouts, and Whitings, otherwise Hidings, and of the fry or young brood thereof! whereby the said Fisheries have been rendeied and are bec ome altogether unprofitable, and nearly useless, to the great hurt and prejudice of the Public, as well as of the individuals interested-therein.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to extend an Act of the Parliament of Scotland in the year 1563, respecting the Salmon Fisheries of that Kingdom, to the Fisheries within the Solway Frith: And that Mr. fames Graham and Sir William Pulteneydo prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Benjamin Weall'ms, according to Order, brought to the Rar, where he received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker; and was ordered to be discharged out of custody, paying his fees.

The Reprimand was as followeth;

Benjamin W’all,

A Select Committee of this House, appointed to try and determine the merits of the Middlesex Election, have reported, That you, having been duly summoned to appear as a Witness before them, disobeyed that summons, and did not attend in pursuance thereof.

It is highly necessary that it should be known and felt, that the Power of this House will at all times overtake and punish all offenders against its just Authority: and you having presumed to disobey that Authority, this House thought fit that for your offence you should suffer imprisonment.

Nevertheless, being willing to believe, according to your own Statement, that your offence proceeded more from ignorance than intention, and accepting your submission, this House has ordered that you be now discharged; and you arc discharged accordingly, paying your fees.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That what has been now said by Mr. Speaker, in reprimanding the said Benjamin Weall, be entered in the Journal of this House.

A Petition of several Merchants, Manufacturers, and Petition others, concerned in the Irish Linen Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners Trade, have observed with concern, that a Duty has lately been laid on the Export of Irish Linen Cloth from Great Britain and Ireland to all Foreign Countries, varying in the Rates from if to 4 per-Cent. upon the value; and that the Petitioners apprehend the direct tendency of this Duty goes to discourage the Linen Export of this Country to Foreign Markets, and to afford of course a proportionate encouragement to the Linens of other Countries, our competitors and rivals; and that a Bill having passed in the present Session for continuing the Duty, and an intention having been expressed of rendering it perpetual, the Petitioners are constrained to offer their tellimony against a measure, the consequences of which they cannot contemplate without apprehensions of the most serious concern; and that Ireland received the Linen Manufacture from Great Britain upwards of a century ago by a solemn Compact between the two Kingdoms, and for a great and valuable consideration, and the Linen Manufacture of Ireland was

thereby exempted, on going into or through Great Britain, from all Duties and Imports, and was likewise of right 1

entitled to every encouragement which Great Britain could afford; and that, conformable to the principle of this Compact, Great Britain continued to act, in all cases respecting the Linen Manufacture of Ireland,until the present in-stance; and that the Legislatures of both Countries, concurring at different periods, did, by a wife system of Bounties, Premiums, and Regulations, lay the broad balls of that extensive prosperity to which the Linen Trade of Ireland has since arrived, as appears by a companion of the 3 Export

44 Gf.o. III. 24° A prills. 225

Export before and since that measure was established; and that the Linens of Ireland are still liable to the fame competition in Foreign Markets which they have always experienced from Foreign fabricks, the rates of Linens being advanced to the Irish Manufacturer from various internal causes, in the proportion of at least 20 per-Cent. in the course of a few years, while* at the same time, the Petitioners have to lament, that, from the year 1796 to the present period (taking one year with another) there appears an annual decrrease in the Exports of no less than ten millions of yards; and that the Petitioners apprehend these facts form a very serious ground of consideration, as relating to an object of some importance in respect to the Commerce of the Empire, and the consumption of Great,

but in the highest degree essential to the dearest interests of Ireland, as affecting its staple and only extensive manu-

facture, the prop of its industry, the nurse of its population, and the main pillar of its credit; and it is for the House to consider, whether it will give effect and continuance to a measure which goes directly to counteract that system, from whence the growth, extent, and prosperity of this valuable Manufacture has so evidently proceeded; and that the Petitioners consider themselves unhappy in being obliged to come forward, at this period, with their prayer against a measure which goes to raile any part of the Public Supplies; but, as in point of Revenue, the amount of this Duty cannot be an object of importance, and the mifchiets arising from it may be of very serious consequence to this Country, and as the House has been plfcaled to entertain exceptions to the generality of the Tax in favour of certain other Manufactures, some of them of great extent and unrivalled excellence (particularly the Cotton Manufactures of Great Britain) the Petitioners hope for a liberal construction of their motives, and that they will not be deemed unreasonable in praying, that the Linen Manufactures of Ireland may, in like manner, be admitted as an exception to this Tax, as the Cotton Manufactures of the United Kingdom already are: And therefore praying, That the House will take the subject matter of their Petition into its serious consideration, and grant such relief in the premises as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Henry Lascelles reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Manufacturers of Woollen Cloth, in the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the lame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Cookson, a Manufacturer of Woollen Cloth in the neighbourhood of Leeds, being examined, said. That he has begn concerned in the Woollen Manufacture about 32 years; and being further examined, said. That heretofore the Woollen Manufacture in the West Riding of Yorkshire,has been carried on in a domestic way by Master Clothiers, who have served regular apprenticeships to the trade, and brought up a vail number of apprentices under them; which Mailer Manufacturers always employed the Poor in their neighbourhood as workmen, and the trade was conducted partly in the Mailers houses, and partly in the workmen’s, and the whole was wrought by manual labour: That within the last twenty years the general trade has considerably increased, and machinery has been introduced, and is now used inalmoll every branch of the manufacture; the use of which machinery, in the preparatory procels of the raw material, is conceived by the Mailer Clothiers, who are now the Petitioners for relief, to be useful in carrying on the trade; but the collecting the looms in large manufactories, where the raw material goes through the preparatory processes, which is becoming very prevalent, will, if not restrained,.tend to destroy the domestic system above described, which has hitherto been preduftive of the mod beneficial effects: That a system, thus beneficial and benevolent, which, in increasing the population of the districts where it exists, at the same time spreads it over the country, and aids and assists rather than impedes the agriculture of it, will be sacrificed, if some remedy is not provided by factory Establishments; and it is the object of the present application to prevent this, for the domestic system is evidently, from the nature of it, of flow growth, and if once destroyed may probably never be revived.—And being aflted. What alteration in the present Laws he conceives to have become necessary for the better regulation of the Woollen Manufacture; he said. That the 27th, 28th, and 32d sections of the Act of the 5th of Elizabeth, cap. 4. requiring the parents of apprentices in the Woollen Trade to be pof-lelled of £.3. per year out of Cities, Towns Corporate, and £. 2 per annum in Cities, operates as a restriction with respect to apprentices, and checks the domestic lyftem,

and ought to be repealed: That the Penalties imposed to enforce and protest the use of apprentices, are so very small, they could not be felt by the wealthy Manufacturer, thou Id he be inclined to transgress the Law, and cannot therefore, unless increased, operate to protest the domestic system by requiring apprenticeships; and the restrictions as to the number of looms appear absolutely necessary, to prevent the large Manufacturers (in whose factories persons not having served apprenticeships are employed indiferi-minately with those who have) from swallowing up and totally annihilating the domestic trade. It is proposed therefore, to increase the Penalties for employing persons not brought up to the trade as apprentices, and to limit the number of looms to be used in the fame house or factory.

And the Witness added. That, as to the numerous Acts which contain provisions with relation to the trade, which have been considered as obfblete, the Petitioners do not presume, for they do not feel competent, to enter into them. It would require a knowledge of the whole trade, as applied to other branches of it, and to other Counties and parts of Great Britain, which they do not profess; and they have therefore confined the application to the evils affecting themselves, which, if not speedily remedied, will put them out of the reach of relief.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Regulation of the Woollen Cloth Manufacture in the County of York: And that Mr. Henry Lascelles and Mr. Wilberforce do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed for the Members of the House.

A Petition of several Members of the Society for bettering the condition of the Poor, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the infectious Fever has been for a long time very prevalent among the Poor of London, the average of those who, during the preceding century, have annually died of that disorder within the Bills of Mortality, having exceeded three thousand; and that this calamity has been continued and increased by the circum-stance of there being many narrow Courts, Lanes, and Paf. sages, and some public Buildings in the Metropolis, from which the infection has not, for manyyears,been expelled by the proper means of purification; and that the Petitioners, and other Members of the Society for bettering the condition of the Poor, having noticed the beneficial eiFefts of the Fever lnftitutionsat Manchester, Waterford, and other places, have endeavoured to form a similar.lnflitution in the Metropolis, and called a meeting, and opened a subscription for that purpose; but the collection has not been adequate to its object, it has, however, been sufficient to establish in Gray's-Inn-Lane a Fever lnfti tut ion, which, though on a contracted scale, has received, and has already cured and discharged, a considerable number of Fever Patients, and has also white-washed and purified several of their habitations in which inteftious Fever had been prevalent; and that some Parishes of the Metropolis have manifested an inclination, and adopted measures, to co-operate with this Institution, but where so large a proportion of the Inhabitants belong to Country Parishes, and are only occafronal residents in Town, the difficulty of providing, in the first instance, an adequate remedy for to inveterate an evil exceeds the ordinary powers of Parish relief; at the same time the interest of Individuals, in any measures to be adopted, is rendered more weak and more distanf, whitft the danger to the Public is greatly augmented, and in fast generally extended, by the constant communication between the Metropolis and every part of the United Kingdom; and that the Society for bettering the condition of the Poor, imprefied with these considerations, and being de-

Ordered, That Mr. Burland do make the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the London Clergy, whose names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and others, Incumbents of Livings, whose income was regulated by an Act, passed soon after the dreadful Fire of London in 1666, was referred.

Mr. Burland accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the lame was read; and is as followeth; •viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Loggen being examined, said. That before the Fire of , the Incumbents of Livings in that City were entitled, under a Decree of Commissioners, made pursuant to an Act of the 37th of King Henry the Eighth, to payments in lieu of Tythes, at the rate of is. 9 in the Pound, on the rents of the houses and other buildings in their respective Parishes; and that, the said Fire having destroyed or damaged eighty-five Parish Churches, it was, by an Act passed in the 2nd year of King Charles the Second, enacted. That thirty-four of the said churches should not be rebuilt, but that the Parishes to which they belonged should be united to others; and, by another Act, of the 22d and 23d year of the fame King, the maintenance of the Ministers of the several Parishes which had suffered by fire, was settled at certain specific yearly sums, in lieu •of Tythes, to be levied by an equal Rate on the houses and other buildings in each Parish respectively, over and above Glebes, Gifts, and Perquisites; and that of the fifty-one Livings which were lb regulated, the incomes of fix only were settled at f. 200 per Annum; thirty-two at less than £.150; and one-fourth of these at no more than £. 100.: And the Witness added. That the income of the several Incumbents being thereby fixed at a very low rate, the lame is, by the decreased value of money, the enhanced price of all the necessaries of life, and other circumstances, become greatly insufficient for the support of their iituation and character.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of certain Incumbents of Livings in the City of London: And that Mr. Burland and Mr. Serjeant Bejl do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Irish currency; and the Petitioner, not having hitherto relided therein, and being desirous of obtaining feme other house for the residence of himself and his successors, and the said piece of ground being capable of being applied advantageously for the Public Service, it has been proposed, on behalf of His Majesty, that the fame should be purchased for the Public Service, at the price of £. 7,000.; and that, in pursuance of such proposal, an agreement has been made between the Lords of the Treasury in Ireland, and the Petitioner, for the purchase and sale of the said mansion-house, offices, and ground, in case they should be enabled so to do, by the authority of Parliament; and that thereupon the Petitioner took such steps, as he was then advised were necessary, for obtaining the sanction of Parliament, but, by a mistake which occurred in the course of proceeding, he has been delayed and prevented from presenting his Petition to the House at an earlier period; and that, as the benefit and convenience intended to be derived from the Petitioner’s application is very material to the Public, and to the Petitioner and his successors, Archbishops of Dublin, it is expedient that a Bill should be passed this present Session, for carrying the purposes of the said agreement into execution: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to present his Petition, notwithstanding the time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills is elapsed.

That the Petitioner is seised in right of his See of Dublin, of a capital Mansion-house, with the Offices, Gardens, and Appurtenances, situate in Kevin-street, in the Liberty of Saint Sepulchres, adjacent to the City of Dublin, called or known by the name of " The Palace of " the Archbishop of Dublin at Saint Sepulchre's," which hath of late years been suffered to go into very great decay, and cannot be rendered fit for the habitation of an Arch-bishop of Dublin without considerable expence; that the piece of ground whereon the said Mansion-house and Offices now stand is of considerable extent, and the fame, with the Buildings now (landing thereon, have been estimated to be of the value of Seven thousand Pounds Irish currency; and the Petitioner not having hitherto resided therein, and beingdefirous of obtaining some other House for the residence of himself and his successors, and the said piece of ground being capable of being applied advantageously for the Public Service, it has been proposed, on behalf of His Majesty, that the fame should be purchased

A Petition of the Linen Merchants of the Towns and neighbourhood of Belfast and Lijburn, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, with extreme concern, the imposition of a Duty on the Exports of lrish Linens to Foreign Countries, now amounting to £.4. per-cent.; and that this Duty will be materially injurious to that great source of Revenue and general prosperity, the staple Manufacture of Ireland; and that the Export of lrish Linens has declined to an alarming extent for the last seven years, at a period too when a general increase of British Exports has been the subject of exultation in Parliament; and the Petitioners therefore entreat the House to coiifider, before this Duty becomes permanent, what may be the farther decline of the Irish Linen Trade in consequence of a Tax incompatible with its prosperity: And therefore praying, That the House will take into their immediate consideration the absolute necelfity of a repeal of this Duty.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Petition of several Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Irish Linen Trade.

Sir John Frederick reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Commissioners for the care, management, and direction, of the Bridge of Stones and Egham causeway, in the Counties of and

was referred j That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for building Bridges, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the 3 til year of His present Majesty, for building a Bridge cross the River 'thanesfrom St ones to Egham, in

the Counties of Middlesex and , was read: And,

Mr. Henry Horne being examined, said, That the Commissioners have proceeded in the execution of the said Act, and built a Stone Bridge, by contract, for the sum of £. 8,400, but which, owing to the piers sinking, was soon after obliged to be taken down: That they afterwards contracted for the building an Iron Bridge, on Stone Abutments, for the sum of £. 4,900. which has been lately completed, but the cracking of several parts of the iron work has since made it necessary, for the public safety, that the lame should be Ihut up, and the old Bridge re-opened: That the expence of the said Bridges, and other works appertaining thereto, have nearly exhausted all the monies which the Petitioners are authorized to raise; and that, in order to enable them to complete and effectually support the said Bridge, it will be expedient that they should be empowered to borrow a further sum, and increase the Tolls, if it should be found necessary.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend an Act, made in the 31ft year of His present Majesty, for building a Bridge cross the River 'Thames, from Stanes to Egham, in the Counties of Middlesex and Surrey: And that Sir John Frederick and Lord William RuJJell do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, House vote That the Thanks of this House be given to the Mod noble Richard Marquess Wellesley, Governor General of the British welletley.ic Possessions in the East Indies, for the zeal, energy, and ability, with which the Military resources of the British Empire in India have been recently applied, under his direction, in the prosecution of the War against the confederate Forces of Scindia, and the Rajah of and

that this House doth eminently attribute the brilliant and glorious successes which have crowned our Arms in that quarter of the Globe to the vigorous and comprehensive system of measures pursued by Marquess for

bringing the various Armies with promptitude and effect into the field;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That the Thanks of this House be given to the Most noble Richard Marquess Wellesley, Governor General of the British Possessions in the East Indies, for the zeal, energy, and ability, with which the Military resources of the British Empire in India have been recently applied, under his direction, in the prosecution of the War against the confederate Forces of Scindia and the Rajah of; and that this House doth eminently attribute the brilliant and glorious successes which have crowned our Arms in that quarter of the Globe to the vigorous and comprehensive system of measures pursued by Marquels for bringing the various Armies with promptitude and effect into the field.

Resolved, That the Thanks of this House be given to the Right honourable Lord Clive, late Governor of the Settlement of Fort Saint George, for his zealous, cordial, and honourable concurrence, in promoting the Military operations which, since the commencement of the War, have been attended in every part of India with an uninterrupted series of the most signal and splendid Victories.;

Resolved, That the Thanks of this House be given to Jonathan Duncan, Esquire, Governor of Bombay, who, by his promptitude and activity in employing the resources and power of that Presidency, has materially contributed to the glorious success of the British Arms in India.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That the Thanks of this House be given to General Gerrard Lake, Commander in Chief of His Majesty’s and of the Company’s Forces in India, for the eminent judgment, active spirit, and invincible intrepidity, manifested by him in the command of the Army serving in Hindostan, by which he has maintained the honour of the British Nation, and reflected such additional luftreon the reputation of the British Arms.

Resolved, Netnine Contradicente, That the Thanks of this House be given to Major General the Honourable Frederick St. John, for his courage and steadiness in fcconding the efforts of the Commander in Chief in Hindostan; and also to Major General the Honourable Arthur Wellesley, for the many important, brilliant, and memorable services, atchieved by him in the command of the separate Army within the Dekan-, and also to the several Officers of the Army, both European and Native, for their gallant con-dust and meritorious exertions during the arduous, honourable, and successful campaign in the East Indies.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That this House doth highly approve and acknowledge the zeal, discipline, and bravery, uniformly displayed by the non-commissioned Officers and private Soldiers, both European and Native, employed against the Enemy in the East Indies-, and that the fame be signified to them by the Commanders of the several Corps, who are desired to thank them for their exemplary and gallant behaviour.

Ordered, That the said Resolutions be transmitted by Mr. Speaker to the Marquess Wellesley, Governor General of the British Possessions in the East Indies, and that his 10 - LorJIhip

Mr. Curwen reported from the Committee, to whom the Hamby Petition of Thomas Quai/e and John , in behalf of Harbour

themselves and the House of Keys of the ljle of Man, and ^pbrud*. of other persons interested in the Trade and Commerce of the United Kingdom; and also the Report of the Commissioners of Inquiry for the Isle of Man, 1792; and also the Paper intituled, " Observations by Mr. Reid," one of the said Commissioners, which were presented to the House upon the 3d day of May 1798, were severally referred;

That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered the lame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr*

George Moore Callow being examined, was asked, If he wa9 acquainted with the Port of Ramsay ? lie laid. He was; that at present it is in very bad state, none but a very small vessel being able to get in, which proceeds from the want of a North Pier; but he believes it is capable of being made a safe and commodious Port; that it has a confide-rabie River that empties itself there, which would facilitate the keeping the mouth of the Harbour open; and that if something is not lhortly done to the Harbour, the Navigation will be entirely impeded.—And being alked, What kind of a Bay Ramsay is ? he said, It is one of the bell in the English Channel, and the belt anchorage, there being no Rocks to impede it.—And being alked, If frequent accidents do not happen to vessels anchoring in that Bay ? he said, They are frequently obliged to cut their cables* and put to feaat great rifle, and being unable to clear the Point of Ayr and Maughlehead, they are driven on (bore, and many lives and much property are annually loft, which would be saved if Ramsay afforded them a secure retreat.—And he further informed Your Committee, That no part of the money granted by Government has been laid out upon the Navigation of Ramsay.—Then,

Edward Christian, Esquire, being examined, said. That he was perfectly well acquainted with the Port of Ramsay; that the last time he saw it was about three years ago, and that it was then in the state described by Mr. Callow; that he thought it capable of being rendered a good Harbour,

3 X if

262

5° Mali. 1804.

if the Sand Bank which bars the Harbour were removed by a North Pier being built to direct the bed of the River; that the depth of the water at Spring tides is from 18 to 20 feet, and at Neap tides from 10 to 13 feet; and that the local situation of Ramsay induced him to think that a good Harbour might be made there, having the advantage of a considerable River, which would clear and keep open the mouth of the Harbour.—And being alked. If the Road-stead of Ramsay is a good one ? he said, A very excellent one; the Southerly winds which generally force the vessels from Liverpool and other Ports to the South, have no effect upon the vessels anchoring there, from the hills which surround the South fide of the Bay; the water in the Bay in Southerly winds is quite calm, comparatively.—And being alked. In what winds is the anchorage insecure in Ramsay Bay ? he said, All those in the North-east to the South-east included; that in those winds it is very dangerous for vessels to get out of the Bay, and that many accidents happen, which he is persuaded would be avoided if Ramsay Port were made capable of receiving vessels of burthen; that many vessels are deterred from flickering themselves in Ramsay from the want of a Port, and knowing the danger if the wind (hoald change to the South-east, East, or North-east; but if the Harbour was improved, the Bay of Ramsay would be more generally frequented as a place of security by all vessels from the Coast of Cumberland, Lancashie, and the Channel.—And being alked, If in his opinion there was any place in the Channel that would afford equal security with Ramsay, if the Pier was built ? he said, None, that he ever heard or fawj that he had often heard seafaring Men and Merchants express their strongest wilh that the Port of Ramsay should be improved so as to afford their vessels a refuge during the winds before described, and would have contributed their pecuniary assistance to accomplish that object; and that the Inhabitants and himself have often been obliged to fend their goods at a considerable expence to Douglas, or Peel, for want of a conveyance from Ramsay.—Then,

John Christian, Esquire, being examined, said. That he Was acquainted with Ramsay, and was there last Summer; that it was then in a very bad state j that to the belt of his knowledge, no considerable improvements have been made in it for some years.—And being alked, If any part of the sums granted by Government has been expended upon this or any other Harbours except Douglas He said, he believed not; he has always understood, that the whole -sum granted, which was /. 24,000, was laid out on the Pier of Douglas.—Then,

Dr. Kelly, d. d. being examined, said, That he saw the Harbour of Ramsay in the month of September last; the Piers were then in a very dilapidated state, and the Harbour itself very inconvenient for the reception of shipping,from a Bar at the Mouth, hardly capable of receiving Herring Boats.—And being alked. If he conceived the Harbour ot Ramsay capable of being made an excellent one ? he said. Yes; having the advantage of a considerable River, which would aft as a Back-water to scour the Channel, and remove the Bar; that the situation of Ramsay was such as would afford general advantage to the Trade of St. s

Channel, if it were made capable of receiving vessels of burthen.—And being alked. If frequent accidents do not occur to vessels flickering there ? he said, Almost always, when an Easterly wind prevails.—And being alked. If the improvement of Ramsay Harbour would not considerably benefit the Island ? he said. Very much.—And he further informed Your Committee, That he was 5 native of the Island, and consequently acquainted with it, and that his observations were the result of long experience.—Then, Edward Christian, Esquire, being again examined, said, That he has known vessels make the passage from Whitehaven to Ramsay, and the reverse, when a passage could not be effected from any other Port in the Island; and he has known the Packet detained at Douglas by winds which would not prevent a passage being made from And being alked. If he was not conversant in Trade ? he said, Hewas.—And being alked, Whether he believed if the Port of Ramsay were made capable of containing vessels of burthen, it would ielien the rate of Insurance from the Coast of Lancashie and Cumberland to ? he said. He certainly

would prefer under-writing a Policy upon those voyages to

Ireland if Ramsay Bay afforded them a secure retreat; and that he thought it would lessen the Insurance.—And,

A Member present informed Your Committee, That there appears to be/. 19,000. and upwards of Balance of the last six years Revenue of the of Man-, and that hitherto the Revenues of the said Island have beeen appropriated to the improvement of the Island, Bounties for Fisheries, and the purposes of the internal Government of the Island; and that/.24,000. granted, as he understands, for the repairs of the Harbours by the Treasury, has been, as he is informed and believes, wholly or nearly lo expended on the Port of Douglas, which, though of great advantage to the Island, is of less importance to the general Trade of the Kingdom than Ramsay. That although the Port of Douglas affords Ibelter in case of storms, the difficulty of getting to Sea with an Easterly wind, makes it less frequented, as vessels are often detained there a considerable length of time when the wind would be fair for them to proceed on their passage. —Then,

A Member present produced to Your Committee two Letters which he had received; the one from Captain J.Huddart, of the Trinity House, and the other from Alexander Shaw, Esquire, Lieutenant Governor of the Isle of Man, of the fame date, relating to the state and condition of the Harbour of Ramsay,which are inserted in the Appendix.

Appendix (A.)

" Dear Sir,

" I am lorry to lay, that it is not in my power to attend the Committee on the improvement of Ramsay Harbour Tommorrow. The improvement of this Harbour, to admit Ships of burthen into iafety, would not only be useful to the place, but afford relief to such vessels as may be in distress. The Bay is a good Road with Westerly winds,-and might be more frequented by Ships navigating St. George'% Channel, if the Harbour is improved. At present if a gale come on so strong from the Eastward, that Ships cannot work out of the Bay (which to those winds it is ex-poled) they mult, if they part their cables, go on Ihore if they have not sufficient accommodation in the Harbour} and therefore, if improved, be materially useful.

I am. Sir,

Highbury Terrace, Your most obedient,

3d May 1804. humble Servant,

John Curzven, Esq. J. Huddart.n

Appendix (B.)

" Sir, Weymou.th-Str3d May, 1S04.

" I have just now received your Letter of this date, in which you do me the honour to alk my Opinion respecting the ufefulneis of having a good Harbour at,

in the Ife of Man. In anl'wer, I do not hesitate to offer it as my lincere Opinion, that such Harbour would be not only beneficial to the I/le of Man, but highly so to the general Trade of His Majesty’s Subjects of the United Kingdom, having occasion at any time to navigate St. George's Channel, and moreespecially in the winter months.

I believe. Sir, that Ramsay Bay is one of, or perhaps the very bell Road Head in the Channel, at least, that it is so considered. I know it is much frequented by vessels of every description, when, either inward or outward bound, they are prevented by contrary winds from proceeding on their respective voyages. It happens, however, not unfre-questly, that to keep as much as they can out of the heavy sea, raised in particular by strong South-weft winds, they are glad to anchor lo near the Ihore as to be in great danger in the case of a sudden change to the Eastward. It mull, therefore, be highly desirable to have always a Port under their lee, in which in case of need to leek and to find shelter; and I have understood that a Pier properly constructed, and at no very great expence, compared to its utility, would give into Ramsay a draught of not less than eighteen feet water or more on Spring tides, and in that proportion less at Neap tides.

I have the honour to be with much esteem.

Sir,

Your most obedient and humble Servant,

John Curzven, Esq. &c. &c. Shaz'J"

A Petition of the Merchants, Ship Owners, and others, in Workington, Harrington, and Maryport, was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth. That there are, in the Cumberland Ports, about five hundred fail of Ships, of very considerable burthen and value, moftof them employed in the Trade to Ireland, and that in the Isle of Man there is not a Harbour fit for the reception of Ships of any considerable burthen, or capable of protecting them in a gale of wind, which deficiency is found very sensibly, and for want of it many valuable Ships and Lives have been loft i and that Ramsay Bay is a place which the Petitioners believe very capable of being made a safe and secure Harbour, at a moderate expence, and if it were done, it would be of very material advantage to the Trade to and from the Cumberland Ports, as well as from Liverpool, the Clyde, or elsewhere, when in the passage it may be necessary to go down the North Channel; and that the erecting a Harbour at Ramsay would be of'considerable benefit to the Isle of Man, and a furtherance of its Trade and Commerce: And therefore praying the House to take their case into consideration, and to give such assistance as may seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

LORD George Augustus Henry reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Owners of Estates, Lands, and Grounds, in the County of Derby; and also, the Petition of several Owners of Estates in the County of Derby, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place •, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’sTable: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Crufo being examined, feid. That the Road leading from Crawford, in the Parish of Wirksworth, in the County of Derby, along the Road to in the same County,

is much out of repair, narrow, and incommodious, and cannot be effectually amended, widened, and kept in repair, by the ordinary course of Law; and that it would be of great benefit and convenience to the neighbourhood, and of public utility, if the said Road was made Turnpike, and powers given to amend, widen, turn, alter, improve, and keep in repair the same; and if a power was also given for making a branch of Road, to lead from the said Road up the Valley between the and Jble, by Grange Mill, to or near to Newhaven House, in the Parish of Hartington, in they feid County; and also, for making, amending, and repairing another new Road branching from the said first-mentioned Road near the said Valley, to the Town of Wirksworth aforesaid.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir William Weller Pepys and Mr. Harvey:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue and render more effectual two Acts, passed in the thirty-third year of his late Majesty, and the twenty-second year of His present Majesty, for layinga Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or one-sixth part of a Penny sterling, on every Scots pint of Ale or Beer brewed for laic, or vended within the ' Town and Parish of Dalkeith; for paving, cleanung, and lighting the Streets of the said Town; and for erecting a new public Market therein; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for empowering the Justices of the Peace for the County of Leicester, at their General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, to make a fair and equal County Rate for the said County; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for amending, and keeping in repair, the Road from the Dudley Turnpike Road, near the House called The Swan Inn, in the Parish of Weft Bromwich, in the County of Stafford, to the House called The Horse and Jockey, in the Parish of Sutton Coldfield, in the County of Warwick', without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for inclosing Lands in the Parish of in the County of Suffolk;without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, That the Lords do request that this House will be pleased to communicate to their Lordships the Evidence upon which they passed the Bill, intituled, An Act for the preventing of Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Aylef-bury, in the County of Buckingham: And also.

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, That the Lords do request that this House will be pleased to communicate to their Lordships, a copy of the Minutes of the Evidence, which were reported to this House, from the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of Ireland, as to its Circulating Paper, its Specie, and Current Coin, and the Exchange between that part of the United Kingdom and Great Britain.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

' Resolved, That this House will fend an Answer to lb much of the Message from the Lords, as relates to the Evidence upon which this House passed the Bill respecting the Aylesbury Election, and also to the Minutes of the Evidence reported to the House from the Committee on the Irish Currency, by Messengers of their own.

And the Messengers were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And then they again withdrew.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by. both Houses, do deftre the immediate attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the deGre of the Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills, and one Private Bill, therein-mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of , their Royal Highnesses the Duke of York, the Duke of Clarence, the Duke of Kent, the Duke of Cumberland, the Duke of Sussex, the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor, the Earl of Dartmouth, and the Lord Hawkesbury, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

Mr. Egerion reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Ieveral Owners of Estates in the Township of Saltney, in the Manor and Parish of Hawarden, in the County of Flint, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Drainage Bills, had not been complied with, by reason that at the time notice was given, in the month of September last, of the intended application to Parliament, there existed no reasonable expectation that either the Tythes of the Sallney Allotments, or the Lands called The Cops, would be included in the provisions of the Bill; but it having been since required, by some of the Proprietors of the Saltney Allotments, that both the Tythes, and the Estate called The Cops, should be assessed with the other Lands, such alteration hath been agreed to by the Rector, and by Sir Stephen Richard , the foie Owner of the said Lands called The Cops-, and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Boydell, being examined, said, That there are within the Township of Manor and Rake, which adjoins the Township of Saltney, certain Lands and Grounds called The Cops, which are under the fame level, and liable to be injured in the same manner, as the Lands in the Township of Saltney; and that it is expedient that the fame should be subject and liable to the powers and provisions of a Bill ordered in for more effectually maintaining and keeping in repair the Embankments, and other works, on the South fide of the Channel of the river Dee, within the Manor and Parish of Hawardine, in the County of Flint; and also, that the Tythes of the Allotments or parcels of Land in,

should be rated and taxed, for the purposes of the said Bill.

Ordered, That, in consideration of the particular circumstances mentioned in the said Report, leave be granted that Notices may be given on the door of the Parish Church of Hawarden, in the County of Flint, for three Sundays in the present month of May, and in the month of June next, that provision will be made in a Bill now depending in the House, for more effectually maintaining and keeping in repair the Embankments and other works on the South fide of the Channel of the River Dec, within the Manor and Pari Hi of Hawardett, in the County of Flint, and for erecting, and keeping in repair, other Embankments and works, to prevent injury being done to the Allotments of Land made, by virtue of an Act passed in the i8ch year of His present Majesty, from a certain Common called Saltney Marsh, for rating and taxing certain Lands and Grounds situate in the Township of Manor and Rake, the sole property of Sir Stephen Richard Glynne, Baronet, called The Cops, according to the value thereof, in the fame proportion and manner, as near as may be, as the said Allotments are intended to be rated and taxed; and for rating and taxing the Tythes arising from the said Allotments.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Frederick Booth being examined, said, That the Churchyards of the said Parish are now so full, that there is not fufli-cient room therein for the interment of the Parishioners; that there is not any proper place within the said Parish that can be appropriated for that purpose; and it would be of great benefit and convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, if a proper piece of ground was provided in a convenient situation in some near or adjoining Parish, to be made ule of as a Cemetery or Burial Ground for the said Parish of Saint Martin in the Fields, and a Chapel erected for performing the Burial Service therein; and that the Petitioners apprehend it may be found expedient to have the c.onstant attendance of a Clergyman to officiate in burying the dead, in which case it will be necessary to erect a proper House for his residence, at or near the said Burial Ground.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Smith and Mr, Ridley.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill* intituled, An Act for more effectually preventing the sale of Exciseable Liquors in Scotland by Persons not duly licensed, and for altering the times of granting Licences to fell such Exciseable Liquors by retail, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enabling the Company of Proprietors of the Thames and Medway Canal to vary the line of the said Canal, and t6 raise a further fufn of money for completing the said Canal and the Works thereunto belonging, and for altering and enlarging the powers of an Act, made in the thirty-ninth and fortieth year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making the said Canal, and collateral Cut thereto; without any Amendment t And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for inclosing Lands in the Manor of Alvecote and ton, in the Parish of Shuttington, in the County of Warwick-, without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Sir John Newport reported from the Committee appointed Report from to consider the Legislative provisions already existing for support of the aged and infirm Poor of Ireland, and for the pXof S punishment of Vagrants, and of the necessity of reviling and amending the Statutes relating thereto, and also of making provision for the care of Lunatics and Idiots by Grand Jury presentments; and to report the fame, with their Observations and Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had examined the matters to them referred; and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with several Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the matters to them referred: And,

Having perused and considered the several Statutes, and examined into such other Evidence relating thereto, as was at the present period laid before them, have come to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the adoption of a general lyftem of provision for the Poor of

Ireland

44 Geo. III. . Vyunii.

311

Ireland, by way of Parish Rate, as in England, or in any similar manner, would be highly injurious to the Country, and would not produce any real or permanent advantage, even to the lower daffes of People, who must be the objects of such support.

, Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the several Acts passed in the Parliament of and parti-

cularly that of the i ith and 12th of His present Majesty, directing the establishment of a House of Industry in every County, County of a City, and County of a Town, have not been complied with, nor any presentment made by the several Grand Juries to assist in the support of such Establishments for the relief of aged and infirm Poor, and the punishment of Vagrants and sturdy Beggars, except in the Counties of Cork, Waterford, Limerick, and Clare, and in the Cities of Cork, Waterford, and Limerick-, but that the House of Industry of Dublin is supported at the public charge, ,$ind is open to the admission of the Poor of the several parts of Ireland, which may have induced the Counties and Cities, that have not carried into effect the establishment of separate Houses of Industry, to consider the House of Industry of Dublin, so regulated and provided for, as a sufficient contribution on their part, and precluding the necelfity of their making farther provision for their Poor.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Act of the 5th of His present Majesty, and other Acts, directing the establishment of Infirmaries or County Hof-pitals, and granting a certain allowance from the Treasury, by way of Salary, to the Surgeon or Physician attending thereon, have been carried into effect in almost all the Counties of Ireland.

Mr, Wilberforce presented to the House, according to whitwood Order, a Bill for inclosing Lands in the Manor and Town- indofureBUl, ship of Whitwood, in the Parish of Feat in the prefcn

West Riding of the County of York: And the fame was received; and read the first time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a second time.

Resolved, That, so far as at present appears to this Committee, the provisions of the Act of the 27th of His present Majesty, cap. 39. empowering Grand Juries to present the sums necessary for support of a Ward for Idiots and Insane Persons, have not been complied with.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in the House of Industry of Dublin,provision is made for the support of upwards of 118 Idiots and Lunatics, in the House of Industry of Cork for 90, in that of Wfor 25, and in that of Limerick for Paupers so afflicted.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the demand for admission of Lunatics and Idiots into all these places greatly exceeds the accommodation or funds appointed for their support j and that it does not appear that any Institution, maintained in any degree at the public expence, exists in any other parts of Ireland for their reception.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the attention and care necessary to the effectual relief of these distressed objects cannot be efficaciously extended to them whiift they are connected with Institutions of a very different nature, and, at the same time, must in a great degree break in upon and derange the orderly regulation of those Institutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the establishment of four Asylums for Idiots and Lunatics, one in each of the Provinces of Ireland (including that of Dublin) placed in as central a situation as possible, to be erected and maintained in such manner as may hereafter be deemed advisable, either by Grand J ury preferments or otherwise, would be a measure highly beneficial.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the consideration of the important objects referred to their examination requires more mature difeuffion than the present advanced period of the Session of Parliament would allow, and further information than they can at present attain, to enable them to form a correct judgment thereon j and that they do therefore recommend to the House, that the further investigation of this subject be resumed at an early period of the ensuing Session, as an object having llrong claims on the attention of the Legislature.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed for the Members of the House.

Petition of Mr. Charles Laurence Dundas reported from the Com-inhabiunts of mittee, to whom the Petition of ‘Thomas Lord;

Hands[ His Majesty’s Lieutenant of the County of Orkney, for

reported. himself, and on behalf of other Owners of Land in the

I (lands of Orkney, and the bumble Petition of James' Chalmer, Esquire, Agent for other Landholders in the said lllands, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the Housej and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the matter of the said Petition:—To prove the Allegations whereof.

The Reverend James Bremner, Miniller of the Parish of Walls and Float a, in the , being examined, laid.

That by the failure of the Corn Harvelts in the lllands of f)rkney,the Inhabitants are reduced to a state of the greatest distress: That the great body of the People, computed to be nearly twenty-four thousand in number, are in absolute want; and, unless immediate relief is afforded, are in danger of perishing: That the crop of the year 1801 was barely sufficient for the consumption of the Country, and to afford the feed for that of the ensuing year; and * that of the year 1802 was so deficient, bath in quantity and in quality, as not to be sufficient to maintain the Inhabitants for a quarter of a year; the country was supplied by an Importation, great beyond all precedent, and more than five times as much as was brought in in 1783, a year of remarkable scarcity: That, to assist in purthaiing this extraordinary supply, the Farmers were obi. geo to Jilpo'e of their Cattle; and by such means, and the aid of their Landlords,who furnished them both with Meal and Grain, they were enabled to subsist, and prepare for the lucceeJing Crop of 1803; unfortunately, that also failed to an alarming extent; the Oat Seed taken from the preceding crop being exceedingly weak, vegetation was checked, and in many instances, altogether destroyed by the inclemency of the weather during the Spring lealon; and though in some Iheltered situations the Bear or Big (a species of Barley mod congenial to the foil and climate) yielded a moderate return, yet in the greater part of the country it was blalted by storms in the Harvest, and the Barley raised from Seed brought from the South of Scotland, and furnished to the Tenants by their Landlords, was lluken, and totally destroyed: That the crop of Potatoes in 1802 and 1803, was also extremely unproductive; and, to add to their calamities, the remaining Cattle became unfaleable: That he left the Orkneys in October 1803, when the state of the crop was such as to induce him to think, that, though not lo deficient as the former years, it would by no means luffice the supply of the Inhabitants: That from what he law of the state of the crop last Autumn on the ground, he was fitisfied that a great part of it was not worth reaping; and finde he left the Orkneys, he has had advice that the country is in the greatest distress, owing to the failure of the last crop, and their inability to purchase a Supply. —Then,

The witness produced to Your Committee, a Minute of the Meeting of the Clergy of , held at Kirkwall the 19th of April last, which is hereunto annexed.

At Kirkwall, 19th April 1804. Several of the Clergy met, in consequei.ee of circular Letters from Mr. Buguid, Vol. 59.

Moderator of the Synod of Orkney} when, having laid before them a Letter from Mr. Nico/fon, Sheriff Substitute, and maturely deliberated on the object thereof; and having communicated, from their personal knowledge, the actual state of their respective Parishes; and having read 1 Letters lent by others, who could not attend; find catife tq represent, That, from the great failure of crop 1802, in consequence of which there was a necessity for importing victual into the Country to the amount of about ,£.25,000; and that the crop of 1803 having also been exceeding deficient, and the leverity of the present Spring having laid the Farmers under the necessity of giving much of their Corn toprelerve the lives of their Cattle; the Country is so exhausted, that, without some public, considerable, and immediate supply, there is the utmost danger of many of the people perishing, or being obliged to emigrate: They therefore judge themselves under the necessity of repre-fenting to the Sheriff Substitute their lense of the alarmii^ situation of the Country; and earnestly request that he, in his official capacity, will take such measures as to him shall appear expedient, for obtaining speedy and effectual aid from Government, in order to remove the consequences of the present pressure, and preserve the lives of numbers of the people.

Signed, in the name of the Meeting, by

Robert Nicolson, Esq. John Duguid, Prefes.

Sheriff Substitute of Orkney.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the (hid Report be printed for the Members of the House.
