A Petition of several Planters, Merchants, Mortgagees, Petition* Annuitants, and others, interested in the British India

Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; taking __________

notice of the Bill for the Abolition of the Slave Trade, at West Indi^n a time to be limited; and setting forth, That the Peti- planter, Uc' tioners have great reason to apprehend, that the agitation of any question respecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in Parliament, will be productive of the raoft serious and alarming mischief in the British West India Colonies; and that the experience of several years, founded on the difaf-trous events which have happened in the Iffand of Saint Domingo, and the present deplorable fituaiion of that Colony, which is reduced to a state of savage anarchy, and where actions of the greatest atrocity are hourly committed, impress forcibly on the minds of the Petitioners the necessity of avoiding all such difeuflions; and that the Petitioners consider, that the avowal of the doctrines connected with the Abolition of the Slave Trade can have no other effect on the minds of uncivilized men, who consider ah Abolition and Emancipation as one and the fame matter, than to destroy all manner of subordination and good government in the British West India Colonies, and to induce the Negroes to make a general struggle for a wild and law-less freedom through defolat ion and blood(hed; and that the said 6ill, if passed into a Law, will be highly injurious ' to the Petitioners, inasmuch as they will thereby be deprived of the supply of Negroes absolutely necessary for the cultivation and improvement of the British Plantations in the West Indies, in which the Petitioners are interested j and that the Petitioners conceive it to be a leading principle of the British Constitution, that no man’s property shall be injured by an Act of the Legislature without full compensation being allowed him, to which, in any such event, the Petitioners hereby interpose their claims; and that the Petitioners, their Ancestors, and Predecessors, have been induced to settle and embark their fortunes upon Estates in the British West India Elands, the cultivation of which have been carried on at greaterifque and expence, in full confidence that the opportunity of obtaining Negro Labourers, so efiential to the support of their Plantations, would not be denied to the Petitioners by the Legislature of this Country, which has, under various Laws, repeatedly, sanctioned and approved the Trade to Africa, by means of which alone such Labourers can be procured; and that the British West India Colonies are of the greatest importance to the Manufactures, Agriculture, Commerce, Navigation, and Revenue, of the British Empire; and it is im-possible that a stake of such immense value as the property inverted in the British West India Colonies, can be affeftea without affecting the Empire at large; and that, the whole system of Colonial Law, respecting property, the provisions of Families, and the securities of Creditors, have been framed, and now rest, upon the faithof the encouragement held out by the Mother Country; and that, if the said Bill for abolishing the Slave Trade shall be parted into a Law, the greatest confusion and uncertainty must arise in every branch of the various interests which are connected with the British West India Colonies, to the absolute ruin of many, and the great injury of all: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law; and that they may be heard at the Bar of the House, by themselves, or their counsel, against the fame.

A Petition of the Corn Merchants of the City of Dublin Petition of was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have noticed, with the mod serious alarm, in the printed Report of the Committee.on the Corn Trade, a proposition in the Table marked B. for raising the Rates for the admission of Irish Corn into Great Britain to nearly the Rates which it is proposed in the said Report to affix for the admission of Foreign Corn; and that such a measure, if carried into effect, would be of the greatest detriment to Ireland, inasmuch as it would confid rably narrow the channel for the admission of one of the principal articles of her Export to the British Markets, thereby diminish that Export, discourage her general Agriculture, lessen her capabilities of Remittance, and consequently increase the difficulties she already labours under of making good her engagements to Great Britain, as is clearly evinced by the general excessive height of the Rates of Exchange between the two Countries: And therefore praying. That whatever measures the House may adopt to protest the Home Markets against the too frequent admission of Foreign or Colonial Corn, that nothing will be done at least to lessen the present intercourse in Com between the two Countries, or to advance the present Rates for the admission of Irish Corn into Great Britain, or of British Corn into Ireland.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Manufacturers, Petition and others, interested in the African Slave Trade from the s^ve^Trade Port of Liverpool, was presented to the House, and read; Bill, from taking notice of the Bill for the Abolition of the Slave Trade, at a time to be limited; and setting forth, That the Petitioners are largely concerned in the said trade, under the authority of various Acts of the Legislature, particularly of several lately passed for its better regulation; and that if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will be grievously injured in their property so embarked, under the solemn faith of the existing Law of the Land; and that a large deiefiption of His Majesty’s faithful and loyal Siibjefts employed in the carrying on such trade would be thrown out of employ, and rendered unable to support themselves and their families: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, of counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a second time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit,

A Petition of John Hart, of BaUymagard, in the Liber- Petition of ties of the City of Londonderry, Esquire, was presented Mr-to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner onu-T \s possessed of considerable Estates, situate chiefly in the Counties of Done gall and Londonderry, and has usually, for many years past, served as a Grand Juror for the said Counties, and in that capacity the Petitioner attended at the last Summer Assizes for the County of Donegal/, the Honourable Luke Fox, one of the Justices of the Court of Common Pleas in Ireland, then presiding as Judge in the Crown Court of the said County; and that a person, named Anderson Dobson, was put on his trial at the said

Assizes, for a misdemeanour, in having procured a Magi-strate to sign an Affidavit, purporting to have been made to account for the clue Expenditure of Public Money in making a Road, without having actually administered the Oath to the person stated to have made the Affidavit, and which person, together with the Petitioner, had been appointed Overseers by the Grand Jury to make the said.

Road; and that he did not at all act or'interfere in making the said Road, but altogether left that business to the

other Overseer so appointed: And that the Petitioner, on the said trial, was called upon, by the said Anderson Dobson,

to bear testimony to his being a man of a fair and honest

character, which testimony the Petitioner did give; and the evidence being closed, Mr. Justice Fox, in charging 1

the Jury who tried the issue, stated what the Petitioner

had sworn, and, in animadverting on his testimony, said,

" But who. Gentlemen, will give a character of this Mr.

" Hart, degraded and di(graced as he is by this transaction,

" which will intail eternal infamy and disgrace on his " posterity ?" though the Petitioner had not, in any manner, been concerned in the t ran fact ion which cauled the said trial; nor was any evidence then, or at any time given, to warrant even a suspicion that the Petitioner could be guilty of such an offence: And that the Jury having retired, remained some time inclosed, when they were sent for by Mr. Justice Fox, and alkcd, if they had agreed to their verdict; and they informed him, that they were divided in opinion, that some of them were for finding the said Dobson guilty, and others were for acquitting him; and thoft that were for acquitting him, said, they had no doubt of his having prevailed on the Magistrate to sign the said Affidavit, without having administered any Oath to the '

person who was stated to have sworn it, which they thought was a bad act, but they did not think he- had been guilty of any such Fraud as was laid in the Indictment,he not having pocketed any thing by it, or w'ords to that effect; and that the Jury having again retired, they were inclosed till about half past seven o’clock in the evening, when Mr.

Justice Fox sent for them, and, on their coming into Court, they said they were ‘ftill divided in opinion; whereupon Mr. Justice Foxdefired them to go back to their Jury-room, and concluded, by saying, if they did not agree in ten minutes, he would adjourn the Court till fix o’clock on Monday morning,it being then Saturday; whereupon the Jury retired, and not having agreed within the time to which they were limited by Mr. Justice Fox, he did adjourn the Court till Monday morning, and proceeded to dinner with the Grand Jury; but, before he got to the head of the Dinner-room, and dinner not having been served, he was followed by the Sub-lheritf, who informed ' him, that the Jury had agreed; to which Mr. Justice Fox 4 replied,

replied, " They may cool their confeiences till flic o’clock " on Monday morning;" and the Jury, being under the necefiitv of remaining enclosed till the Monday following, and having again returned to their former opinions in con-fiequence of their confinement, they were on that day conveyed to the verge of the County, and discharged by the said Judge; and that he was ndt present in Court at the time when Mr. J u ft ice Fox used the expressions above dated reflecting on the Petitioner, and, not being informed of it, the Petitioner, early on Sunday morning, waited on the Judge at his lodgings, where he found him accompanied by the Clerk of the Crown: The Petitioner said, that he came to make a request which he hoped would not be considered unreasonable, as the business of the Grand Jury was over, and nothing remained for them to do but to pass the presentments: Mr. Justice Fox asked, "Pray, Sir, " what is it i" to which the Petitioner answered, That he hoped he would permit him to return to Derry on that day, as he had ordered a meeting of the 'Inhabitants of the Lower Liberties of Derry, by public advertisement, at twelve o’clock on the next day, for the purpose of forming a Corps of Yeomanry for the defence of the Country. Mr. Justice Fox thereupon said, " Sir, you know your duty, " and I know mine; your attendance to morrow is indif-" penlably necessary upon which the Petitioner retired; and Mr. Justice Fox having gone into Court about a quarter of an hour after lix o’clock on the Monday (which was the 29th of August last) directed that the Crown Solicitor should be called; and he having appeared, Mr. Justice Fox adarelled him in these words: " Go, Sir, and do as I " directed you yesterday;" upon which the Crown Solicitor went out of Court, and took one William Chambers', the Conservator of the Roads (who had been the principal Prosecutor of Dobson) with him; the Grand Jury (amongst whom the Petitioner attended) having been previously called over, and attending in Court, the Crown Solicitor and Chambers having shortly afterwards returned, and Mr. Justice Fox thereupon ordered a Magistrate, who was then standing in Court, to take Chambers'% examination against the Petitioner, and an information, ready drawn our, was then produced by the Crown Solicitor, which information, the Petitioner has reason to believe, was prepared by the -instrudion, and under the immediate authority and direction of Mr. Justice Fox himself; and that the Crown Solicitor having handed the information to the Magistrate who had been ordered to take it, the Magistrate was proceeding to read it, conceiving it his duty so to do before he should examine and swear any person to the truth of its contents; upon which Mr. Justice Fox reprimanded him for so doing, and would not permit him to read it, which induced the Magistrate to express surprize that he should be ordered to take or subscribe an information which he had not read previous to its being sworn: however, by the command of the said Judge, the Magistrate administered the usual oath, and took the said information; and that as soon as the information was thus sworn, Mr. Justice Fox turned towards the Grand Jurors (with whom the Petitioner then was) and said, lie had much concern in calling the attention of the Grand Jury to another subject of much moment; that a Member of the Grand Inquest of the County stood charged before him with a yery atrocious offence; he then proceeded to state, that An Dobson had been put upon his trial before him on Saturday, and he detailed very minutely the evidence which had been given on the trial; he said, that after the evidence had been closed, and the trial over, Mr. Hart had come on the table of himself (which the Petitioner denies to have been true, the Petitioner having been called on by the said Dobson in his defence) to give a character of the Traverfer; and that when he came to animadvert to the Petit Jury on that part of the evidence so given by the Petitioner, he had thought it his duty to say, *• Who, Gentlemen, would give a character " of this Mr. Hart,degraded and disgraced as he was by an " infamous crime, by which he had intailed disgrace on " his posterity, and infamy on his character and name ?" Mr. Justice Fox then proceeded to apply the evidence so Rated by him to have been given against Mr. Dobson to the Petitioner, and Rated, that in consequence of such flagrant conduct, he had directed the Crown Solicitor to prosecute VOL. 59.

him; and, an examination having been (worn, he must order him into tlje Dock, and desired the Sheriff to take the Petitioner into custody, whereupon the Petitioner was taken into custody by the Subfheriff, and placed in front of the Bar, where Traverfers usually Hand for trial; which being perceived by Mr. Justice Fox, he directed that the Petitioner should be put to the Bar, in consequence of which direction the Subsheriff then put him in the place where Felons are arraigned, and receive sentence; and the Petitioner being placed in that degrading situation, and standing as a convicted Felon about to receive the judgment of the Law, Mr. Justice Fox contumelioufiy asked him, " What have you, Sir, to say ? you are now at liberty " to go on," addressing him in the style and manner as if he were really a convicted Felon; but the Petitioner being so affected and confounded by an add re fs so violent and unex-peded, and from being placed in so public and so degrading a situation, could at first icarcely articulate a word with an audible voice, but having recovered a little from his embarrassment and distress of mind, he did mak^ a few observations, after which he was obliged to listen silently to a mod reproachful address from Mr. Justice Fox, who* whilst the Petitioner was in custody, untried, and in the hearing of those whose duty it would be to put the Petitioner upon his trial, and to decide upon his guilt or ^innocence, and holding up the Petitiofler to the resent-ment and indignation of his Country, amongst other things, addressed the Petitioner in the following words: " You " have charged me, as a Judge sent to administer Justice, " with criminal conduct, because I have directed you " should be put upon your trial for a mod infamous crime. " Whether the agitation in which 1 fee you, proceeds from " a sense of insulted honour or detected guilt, from a " wounded spirit or habitual depravity, I know not; but " I can only attribute your conduct to a hardened sense " of being used to such malpractices. A charge of the " mod enormous nature is made against you, disgracing " the Grand Inquest of the Country, not in their persons, " but yours." Mr. Justice Fox, in the course of his address, expressed his determination of returning the en-suing Circuit for the express purpose of trying the Petitioner, and, in the hearing of the Grand Jury, declared, that if they should hesitate in finding the Bill of Indictment, he would direct the Solicitor for the Crown- to apply to the Court of King’s Bench for an information against the Petitioner; and that Mr. Justice in furtherance of such his avowed determination to return next Circuit for the purpose of trying the Petitioner himself, desired that his lodgings should be kept for him; and that, after he had remained some time in the Dock, without knowing what Mr. Justice Fox's further intentions were, or for what alledged crime or offence the Petitioner was then committed, and placed in the common Felons Dock, Mr. Justice Fox informed the Petitioner, that, as it was then too late to have an Indictment prepared, the Petitioner might give bail, and directed that the Petitioner should be bound in £. 1,600, and two sureties in £.500. each, for the Petitioner’s appearance to take his trial at the ensuing Assizes for the offence contained in the said examination, which the said Judge would not suffer to be read, or even dated, but which offence, be it what it might, the said Mr. Justice Fox had prejudged, and pronounced the Petitioner to have been guilty of. The Petitioner, therefore, entered into such security, and was accordingly released, but remained fobut a short time; for, thortly after the Petitioner was so released, the said Judge did again order the Petitioner to be taken again into custpdy, on an Allegation that the Petitioner had entered into some conversation with some of the Jurors after they had been locked up for the purpose of considering their verdict^ on the trial of the said Dobson, and directed the Petitioner to be prosecuted for such offence, and accordingly the Petitioner, at the ensuing Assizes, was tried and acquitted of such charge; and that the Petitioner attended, as he was bound, at the ensuing Affixes, and no Bill having been sent up against the Petitioner for the said alledged offence, for which the Petitioner had been so committed to the Felons’ Dock by Mr. Justice Fox, the Petitioner instructed his counsel to ask the Crown Solicitor, in Court, on the second day of the Assizes, whether the pro-4 O fecution

That the Petitioners have observed, with the most serious apprehension, in the printed Report of the Committee on the Corn Trade, a proposition to raise the Average Prices at which Irish Corn is admissible into Great Britain, and that this measure, if carried into effect, would operate nearly as a prohibition to the Export of Grain to Great Britain ? And therefore praying. That the alterations proposed in the said Report may not pass into h Law.

A Petition of Frances Isabella , of Yokes Place, near Tunbridge, in the County of Kent, Widow, Committee of the Estate of William Dalifon, Esquire, a Lunatic, and John Blundell, Clerk, was presented to the House, and

read } setting forth, That there are within the Lordship of Manton, otherwise Mannton, in the County of Lincoln, several Open and uninclosed Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Leys, Arable and other Grounds, and likewise divers ancient inclosed Lands, Grounds, and Homesteads; and that, if the said Open Lands were inclosed, they might be much improved, and it would be further beneficial to the Petitioners, if such parts of the said Lands as are subjecb to Tythes were exonerated therefrom, and a proper compensation made in lieu thereof; and that the Petitioner, the said Frances Isabella Master, was only lately enabled to enter into an arrangement respecting the said Inclosure, the late Tenant having held the whole of the said Lordship under an agreement which the Petitioner was not enabled to put an end to till the death of the said Tenant, pending which Agreement no Inclosure could have been made with a due advantage to the said Lunatic’s interest, and difficulties having occurred in settling the terms of the said Inclosure, the lame could not be adjusted so as to enable the Petitioners to give the Notices required, or to present a Petition for effecting such Inclosure, before the time limited for receiving Petitions for Private Bills had elapsed: Vol. 59.

And therefore praying, That leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for leave to bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That, in consideration of the particular circum- Leave given.' stances let forth in the said Petition, leave be given to present a Petition as desired.

A Petition of John Dayman, late Under Sheriff of the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was Under Sheriff of the said County on the 9th day of March last, when an election took place for a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Lijkeard j and that the Petitioner, as such Under Sheriff, did, through inexperience in such matters, make a double return, contrary to his duty, and in violation of the Privileges of the House, for which he is extremely concerned, and humbly asses pardon for the fame: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to accept this his submission, and order him to be discharged.

Ordered, That the said Mr. John Dayman be brought to the Bar of this House Tommorrow, in order to his being discharged.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir William Weller and Mr. Harvey:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for altering and amending l'everal Acts for making and repairing Turnpike Roads, in the County of Haddington; for amending other Roads branching therefrom; and for rendering more effectual the Statute Labour within the said County; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the term and powers of two Acts, of the fifth and twenty-sixth years of His present Majesty, for amending the Road from the North end of Old Gate, in the Town and Borough of Malton, to the Town of Pickering, in the County of York; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for reviving the term, and continuing, altering, and enlarging the powers of two Act?, passed in the thirty-second year of his late Majesty, and in the 3d year of His present Majesty, so far as the same relate to repairing and widening the Road from the Town of Derby, to the Town of eter, in the County of Stafford-, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for altering, amending, and consolidating several Acts, for making and repairing Turnpike Roads in the Counties of Renfrew, Lanark, and Ayr; repairing other Roads branching therefrom; and amending an Act. passed in the thirty-second year of His present Majesty, for making effectual the Statute Labour in the County of Renfrew, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill* intituled, An Act for making and maintaining a Railway qr Tram-road from the Town of Swansea,into the Parish of Oystermonth, in the County of Glamorgan; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend two Acts, made in the eighteenth and thirty-ninth years of His present Majesty, for the erecting a Court House for the holding of Sessions of the Peace in the City of Westminster, and for purchasing certain Buildings and

Ground between Saint Margaret Street, Union Street, and

King Street, in the said City, for the use of the Public; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for inclosing Shaddingfield Common, in the County of Suffolk; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for inclosing Lands in the Parish, Townships, or Hamlets, of Bringhwjl, Great Easton, and Drayton, in the County of

Leicester; with forne Amendments} to which Amendments the Lords desire the concurrence of this House: And also. The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for inclosing Lands in the Parish of Simonbiirn, in the County of Northumberland; with an Amendment j to which Amendment the Lords desire the concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The Reprimand was as followeth;

Mr. John Dayman,

A Select Committee of this House, appointed to try and determine the merits of the last return for the Borough of IJfkeard, have reported. That you, being Under Sheriff of the County of Cornwall, in annexing to the Writ the Indenture complained of by the Petition of Mr. Hujkijfon, acted contrary to your duty, and in violation of the Privileges of Parliament: upon this charge you have been Jieard •, and the House, after hearing you, has resolved. That you are guilty of the offence laid to your charge, and has ordered you into the custody, where you now are.

The office of Sheriff is a trust of the highest importance to the Parliamentary Constitution of this Country; the impartial execution of its duties is indispensably necessary to the preservation of the Rights and Privileges of this House; and. all practices employed to falsify or delay the returns of Members to serve in Parliament demand the * severest examination.

Your professional education and general habits of life ought to have made you acquainted with the duties of the office which you undertook, or you should have abstained from it altogether; besides which, it is but too plain, from the fads in evidence, that your attention was awakened at the time to the illegality of the ad which you proceeded deliberately to commit.

This House nevertheless, in consideration of your alledged inexperience in such matters, and the contrition which you now feel for your offence; and hoping, that the public notice which your case has at traded may operate as a fa-lutary warning to others upon whom the like duties may devolve, has ordered that you be now discharged; and you are discharged accordingly, paying your Fees.

Ordered, Nemine Contradic That what has been now said by Mr. Speaker, in reprimanding the said Mr. John Dayman, be entered in the Journal of this House.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Crinan Canal, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That in consequence of various Persons having subscribed the sum of £. 107,800, and on their application to Parliament, an Act was passed in the 33d year of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from Loch Gilp to Loch Crinan, in the Shire of Argyll-, and that the work was begun in 1794, and carried on during the several years lince elapsed, but greater difficulties were found in the execution than had been expected, and, in the mean time, the great rife which took place in wages, and in the price of materials, augmented the expence so as greatly to exceed the Estimates; and that, owing to the pressure of the times, many of the Subscribers became unable to pay their Subscriptions, by which the Funds were diminished £. 15,250.; and that in consequence of

this defalcation, the Petitioners, on the Bond of some individual Subscribers, obtained, in the year 1795, a credit from the Briti/k Linen Company, whereon there was advanced, to the 31st of December 1803, £.5,027. 4J. which, with the Interest since accrued, mull be paid immediately; and that the Petitioners, in 1799, applied to Government for a Loan, to enable them to finish this Canal, and an Act passed, authorizing the Barons of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland to advance £. 25,000. out of the Money arising from the sale of the Forfeited Estates in Scotland, for which a preferable security exists on the said Canal; and that the Petitioners, having obtained another Act in 1799, to enable them to raise mors money, several

of the original Subscribers did advance, under the authority of that Act, the sum of £.9,900.; and that the money already expended on this National Work amounts to £. 140,610.-13 r. of which sum the Subscribers have furnished £.98,336. 15.1. \e>d.without having received any Interest upon their advances: the remainder has arisen from the Loans from Government, and from the British Linen Company, from new Subscriptions, and from Tolls collected on the Navigation, and there is due to several Contractors and others £. 5,403. 9 or thereabouts;

and that the Governor and Directors of the said Company, in order to ascertain what sum would still be necessary to completely finish the said Canal, directed Mr. Thomas ford, Engineer, last Summer, to inspect the whole work, and make a Report; and after such inspection, he did communicate to Mr. William Jeffop, Engineer, all the fafts and information he was able to collect; and these two Engineers have made a joint Report, by which it appears that the sum of £.12,787. will be required for finUhing the Canal, and for making a Dry Dock at for repairing

Ships; and that the Petitioners have, in vain, endeavoured to raise amongst themselves, or by borrowing the money necessary for completing the Canal, and paying the British Linen Company, and their other Creditors, and are therefore induced to lay their case before the House, hoping that if it shall be made appear that the said Canal is particularly entitled to the aid of Parliament, and that there is no other means of completing it but by a Public Loan, their application for such aid will be favourably received: And that the Canal has been made of large dimensions, being twelve feet deep on the fills of the locks, for allowing Sea-built Vessels, carrying from 200 to 250 tons, to pass freely; and that the Canal was opened, for the passage of Vessels, on the 18th of July 1801, but at that time it was not safe to fill it with water to a greater depth than eight feet, and Vessels of above 80 tons have since passed; but, as some works are necessary to make the entrance to the Canal safe at the East end from Loch and as there is a want of the full depth of water, the number of Vessels passing the Canal have not yet been so great as there is reason to believe it will be when all the obstructions are removed; and that, from inspection of the Map of Scotland, it will appear, that by means of this Canal, Vessels can pass from the Westward to and from

to the Atlantic, without making the circuit of the Mull of Cantyre, which requires different winds and tides, and by which Vessels have often been detained for many weeks, whereas by the Crinan Canal they will be always sure of a passage in a few hours; and that this Canal will also be of great benefit to that National object the Herring Fishery, because Bufles and Vessels on the East fide of the Island can pass by the Forth and Clyde Navigation to the Crinan Canal, and can, with certainty, arrive at the Fishing-grounds on the North-weft Coasts of Scotland in a very short time, without depending on changes of wind, and in like manner Vessels can pass from the Westward to the Eastern Fisheries; and that by this Canal, a direct and short communication will be opened from all the Western islands and the North-weft Coast of Scotland to Glasgow, and thence to Leith and Edinburgh, for conveying the various commodities produced in those quarters, and for the conveyance back to theft Western places of Coal for fuel, and of Lime for the cultivation of Land, which they arefo much in want of; but above all, that this commmuni-cation will connect, in a very important manner, with the intended Inland Navigation from the Eastern to the Western Sea by Inverness and Fort William, which it will join, and by which means Ships, going to or coming from Ireland and the Weft of England in the Baltic Trade, will have a lufe passage, without being exposed to the severe gales and heavy seas from the ocean when going Northward, or coming Southward; and that this National Work might have been profitable to the Subscribers, if they had made the Canal of small dimensions, but they were desirous that it might answer for large Vessels engaged in Foreign Trade, by which the expence was so very much increased, as to leave them a small prospect of any reasonable interest for their money, unless, by the good effects it shall produce to the community, the traffic by this Canal shall very much increase: And that the Governor and Directors have Vot. 59.

been at pains to ascertain what may be eXpefted to be the amount of Tolls when the Canal is completed; and from the best authority they have reason to believe, that, at the rate of Tolls allowed by the Act, they will amount to nearly £. 9,000 annually; and that the Revenue which the Petitioners believe the Canal will produce, according to a reasonable proportion of the species of goods and commodities now carried by sea, and which cannot fail to pass by it, will be an ample security to the Public for the additional Loan for which the Petitioners are obliged to apply. They might i perhaps have been justified in requesting a grant of Public I Money, instead of which they only apply for a further Loan, in,order to enable them to complete a work from which, even when finished, they, as Subscribers, expect to derive but little benefit, in comparison with that which will accrue to the Public; and that, on the other hand, if the Canal should be (topped, and go to ruin for want of the additional Loan now requested, the community will not only be deprived of the great advantages which would arise from it to Commerce, to the fisheries, and to the improvement of the Western islands and North-weft Coast of Scotland, but the money which by Parliament has been already furnished the Petitioners as a Loan must be entirely loft; and that the Petitioners, for various reasons, could not obtain the consent of the Lords of the Treasury to this application till after the time appointed by the House for receiving Private Petitions had elapsed, and it will be a great lo(s to the Petitioners and to the Public, if this business is delayed till next Session of Parliament: And therefore praying the House for leave to present a Petition, for the above purposes.

•Ordered, That, in consideration of the particular cir- Leave given, cumstances set forth in the said Petition, leave be given to present a Petition as desired.

Sir Thomas Charles Bunbury reported" from the Com- Recommit-mittee, to whom the Report was re-committed, which was made from the Committee, who were appointed to rej,'0nrtei e’ consider of so much of the (evcral Petitions of Land Owners, Barley Growers, Maltsters, and others, in the Counties of Norfolk, Suffolk, Stafford, and Lincoln, which were presented to the House upon the 15th and 29th days of February, and the 28th and 29th days of March last, as relates to an Act, passed in the 31ft year of His present Majesty, for regulating the Importation and Exportation of Corn, and the Payment of the Duty on Foreign Corn imported, and of the Bounty on British Corn exported, and to report th*> fame, with their Obfer-4 S vations

y

342 14° JunA. 1804.

vations thereupon, to the House; and to whom the several Accounts and Papers, which have been presented to the House in the present Session of Parliament, respecting Corn, Grain, and Malt, were referred; That the Committee had made a further Enquiry touching the matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as follow-ethj viz.

Your Committee have, in pursuance of the Instructions which they received, proceeded to examine the Act of the 31st of the King, and to take, from the best information they could obtain, a Comparative View of the Price of Labour, and of the unavoidable Expences incident to the Grower, in the year 1791, and at this time; as the best criterion by which they might judge of what ought to be the price of the different l'pecies of Grain, allowing to the - Grower such a fair and reasonable profit, as may induce him to pursue that line of husbandry which will the most contribute to the production of such an ample supply of the different kinds of Com and Grain, as may be sufficient for our consumption. This suppty cannot be expected without a considerable surplus, in plentiful years, above the demand of the Home Market; it therefore becomes definable that the Grower should have such a ready sale for that surplus by Exportation, and Bounty if requisite, as may remove all apprehension of his not being able to obtain, from a glut of the commodity at the Home Market, such a price for that surplus as will afford him an equitable profit on his labour, industry, and capital, employed in its production. It appears, then, to Your Committee, that the surest mode by which an ample supply can be expected, is to endeavour to secure an uniform and reasonable price to the Growers.

Your Committee find, That the Act passed in 1791, giving a power to the King in Council, when Parliament is not fitting, of prohibiting the exportation of Corn, if the average price thereof, taken from the Return of the whole Kingdom, is higher than the price at or above which Foreign Corn of the fame fort is allowed to be imported at the Low Duties; and to permit generally, for three months certain, the Importation of such fort on the lowest Duties then payable, ought never to be exercised but upon a strong and incontrovertible necessity; as it may otherwise operate as a great discouragement to the growth and production of Corn in this Kingdom, by rendering the Market uncertain, by making the Export Trade liable to be flopped, and by enabling a general Import of Foreign Corn to be poured into the Kingdom for the term of three months, at so small a variation and advance of price in the Home Market, as may perhaps be occasioned for the purpose of producing that effect.

Your Committee are cautious of recommending a repeal of that part of the Act, left a necessity for the exercise of that power might possibly arise, thinking it better under such circumstances, that it should be exercised according to Law, than in opposition to it: in full confidence, that by due encouragement to the Agriculture of the Country, and by bringing the Crown and Waste Lands into cultivation, the produCV of the growth of Corn in the United Kingdom will afford such regular and ample supply for its consumption, as to admit the repeal of that power given to His Majesty’s Privy Council, without the danger of any detriment arising therefrom to the Public.

It appears to Your Committee, That the price of Corn from 1791 to the harvest of 1803, has been very irregular, but upon an average, increased in a great degree by the years of scarcity, has in general yielded a fair profit to the Grower. The casual high prices, however, have had the effect of stimulating industry, and bringing.into cultivation large tracts of Waste Land, which, combined with the two last productive seasons, and other causes, have occasioned such a depression in the value of Grain, as it is feared will greatly tend to the discouragement of Agriculture, unless maintained by the support of Parliament.

Your Committee therefore recommend the Tables hereto annexed, marked (A.) and (B.) to be adopted instead of those in the Act of the 31st of the King, as more fitted to the circumstances of the present times, except so far as relates to the Import and Export from and to Ireland; and Your Committee recommend as a necessary measur, that the Import to Ireland from Foreign parts, and the Export from Ireland to Foreign parts, should be regulated at the same time upon the fame scale, and to a proportionate amount, as in the annexed Tables, calculated on Irish measure, and in Irish money.

It appears further to Your Committee, That the aggregate average prices of the twelve Maritime Districts of England, and of the four Maritime Districts of Scotland, as particularized in the Act of 1791, is the proper rule by which the Tables for regulating the Import of Corn into Great Britain ought to be governed, and that the Export from each District should continue to be governed, as it now is, by the regulations of that Act; and that the Duties payable on Foreign Corn imported into any District where the average price thereof is below the aggregate average price of the twelve and of the four Districts respectively, should be governed by the average price of such District, pursuant to the annexed Tables, and ascertained by the Act of 1791.

Your Committee have been induced to make an alteration in the proportion of the Export prices of Barley, from its being subject to increased Taxation, from which other Grains have been exempt; and further state, that it appears to them, that there has been a balance in favour of Barley for the last thirty-four years, while the balance has been in favour of the Importation of Wheat and Oats. From this circumstance. Your Committee have drawn the conclusion, that that immediate Relief will not be afforded to the Growers of Barley, which it is conceived the Growers of Wheat will receive, by the alterations in the Importation Table.

The object of Your Committee, in fixing the price at which the Ports shall be open for the general Importation of Corn so much higher than the price at which it is permitted to be exported, is to encourage the surplus of one District to be tent for the supply of another in want of ir, that the Import into one part of the Kingdom, and the Export from another at the same time, may thereby be checked, and the prices throughout the Kingdom be made more equal.

With this view, Your Committee recommend the adoption of measures calculated to promote the interests of the Grower, conceiving that a due encouragement to Agriculture is the best and most effectual mode of ensuring to the Consumcr an adequate and regular supply, at a reasonable rate, as well as of obviating those frequent fluctuations in price so injurious both to the Grower and the Public; and also in future to secure to this Country, as far as poflibie, the advantage of such enormous sums, as Your Committee find, have exceeded Thirty Millions in the last thirteen years, which sums, employed in the purchase of Corn abroad, cannot fail to have operated as a Bounty upon the Agriculture of Foreign Countries, to the detriment of our own: whereas it appears by the Corn Returns, that in the course of years when the regulations were most favourable to the Growers, and when the lead check was put upon the trade, the Export of Corn from this Kingdom, for more than sixty years in succession, produced annually Six or Seven hundred thousand Pounds, leaving besides, at a regular moderate price, an ample sufficiency for the Home consumption.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Bigg js an inferior species of Barley; that ic is principally grown in Scotland, in situations improper for the growth of a better lort of grain; that in ordinary years it is used for the purpose of making Malt, but that in seasons unfavourable to the ripening of Oats, it is the chief resource of the Inhabitants for food: It is therefore the Opinion of this Committee, that it would be impolitic to discourage the cultivation thereof, by imposing the lame rate of Duty on Malt made from that article, as from or Scotch Barley.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there ought to be a deduction from the Duties imposed in 1802 and 1803, in favour of Scotch Bigg, to the amount of one-third thereof.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, on the average of twelve years prior to 1804, the Barley of Scotland was inferior, in point of price, to the Barley of England, at the rate of 7 2 id. per quarter, or to the

amount of 19? fer-centum', and that the difference, in point of Duty, is at present at the rate of 15 per-centum. Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table. Ordered, That the said Report and Appendix be printed for the Members of the House.

A Petition of William of the City of,

Victualler, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner is now in the custody of the Serjeant at Arms for improper conduct before the Committee on the Middlesex Election, and that he is fully convinced of the heinousness of his offence, and humbly alks pardon for the fame; and that his wife is now in so advanced a Hate of pregnancy, as to be unable to tranlaCl any business, and he has no one besides to assist him; and that his trade requires the moll conllant attention, and his absence from it, for any length of time, would involve him in inevitable ruin: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to order him to be discharged.

Ordered, That the said William Ilett be brought to the Bar of this House, in order to his being discharged.

William Ilett was accordingly brought to the Bar, where he received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker; and was ordered to be discharged out of custody, paying his Fees.

Petition of William Urn, to be djicharged.

Reprimanded

and discharged#

The Reprimand was as followeth; viz.

William Ilett,

A Select Committee of this House, appointed to try and determine the merits of the Middlesex Election, have reported, That you, having been duly summoned, did not attend the said Committee; and that afterwards, when you appeared before them, you were guilty of gross milbeha-viour; for that cause you were by them committed to the custody of the Serjeant at Arms, and in his custody this House ordered you to remain.

Your conduct appears to have been contumacious in the extreme, regardless alike of the Authority of this Houl'c, and of the proper deportment to be observed by every man who is called upon to give his testimony upon oath in Courts of Justice.

Such misbehaviour demands severe reprehension; but, by the fobmission you have now made, and the charges and inconveniencies you have suffered by your imprisonment, it is hoped that you have received a sufficient admonition to make you, lor the rest of your life, pay a prompt and respectful obedience to the Laws of your Country.

This House has ordered, that you be now discharged; and you are discharged accordingly, paying your Fees.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That what has been now said by Mr. Speaker, in reprimanding the said William Ilett, be entered in the Journal of this House.

Mr. Robert Dundas reported from the Committee, to Crinan Canal whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Crinal Canal, was referred; That the Committee had ex- T amined, and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, it not being intended to give power for railing any further or additional Rates, Tolls, or Duties, or for varying the line of the Canal; and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House j and he read the Report in his place 1 and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read j and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the thirty-third year of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from Loch Gilp to Loch Crinan, in the Shire of Argyll, was read: And,

John Seton Karr, Esquire, Secretary to the Company of Proprietors of the said Canal, being examined, laid, That the Canal was begun in the year 1794, and carried on durt ing the several years since elapsed; but greater difficulties were experienced than had been expectea, particularly from the hardness of some rocks in the line, and from the shifting or loose nature of some land banks, which protracted the execution of the work; and, in the mean time, the great rife which took place in wages, and in the price of materials, augmented the expence lb as greatly to exceed the Estimates:

That, owing to the pressure of the times, many of the Subscribers became unable to pay their Subscriptions, by which the Funds were diminished £.15,250*

3 fhat.

A. 1804

364

25° Ju

• ‘ That, in consequence of this defalcation, the Company, on the Bond of •Tome individual Subscribers, obtained, in the year 1795, a credit from the Linen Company,

whereon there was advanced to the 31st of December last £.5,027. 41. which, with the interest since accrued thereon, tnuft be paid immediately, as the fame has been called for by the said British Linen Company:

That in the year 1799, an Act passed, on the recital of the said Canal being a work of considerable National Importance, authorizing the Barons of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland to advance £. 25,000, bearing interest, out of the money arising from the sale of Forfeited Estates in Scotland, for which a preferable security exists on the Canal: That the Company having obtained another Act in the year 1799, to enable them to raise more Money, several of the original Subscribers did advance, under the Authority of that Act, the sum of £.9,900:

That the money already expended on the above National Work amounts to £.140,610. 135. of which liim the Subscribers have advanced £.98,336. 15 10 without

having received any interest; that the remainder has arisen from the Loans from Government, and from the British Linen Company, from new Subscriptions, and from Tolls collected on the Navigation; and that there is due to several Contractors and others, £. 5,403.' 9 5 d. or there-

abouts.

The Witness produced a Report on the said Canal, made by Mr. Thomas ’Telford and Mr. William JeJfop, by which it

appears, that the sum of £.12,787 is required for finishing the work.

And being further examined, he laid, That the Company have in vain endeavoured to raise amongst them-lelv.es, or by borrowing, the money necessary for completing the Canal, and paying the British Linen Company and their other Creditors:

That the said Canal has been made of large dimensions, being twelve feet deep on the fills of tile locks, for allowing Sea-built Vessels carrying from 200 to 250 tons to pass-: That the Canal was opened for the passage of Vessels on the 18th of July 1801; but at that time it was not safe to fill it to a greater depth than eight feet, and Vessels of above 80 tons have since palfed:

That, by means of the said Canal, Vessels can pals in a few hours from the Weft ward to , and from

to the Atlantic, without making the circuit of the Mull of

Cantyre, which requires different winds and tides, and by which Vessels have often been detained for many weeks; and it will allb be of great benefit to that National object the Herring Fishery, because Busses and Vessels in the Eift fide of the Island can pals by the Forth and Clyde Navigation, and by the said Canal, and arrive at the Fishing-grounds on the North-weft Coast of and

verfd, in a very short time, without depending on changes of wind:

That, by the said Canal, a direct and short communica--tion is opened from the Western Islands and the North-weft Coast of Scotland to. Gl, and from thence to Leith and Edinburgh by the Forth and Clyde Navigation, for conveying the various commodities produced in those quarters, and for the conveyance back to these places of Coal for fuel, and of Lime for the cultivation of land, which they are much in want of:

That the said communication will connect, in a very important manner, with the intended Inland Navigation, from the Eastern to the Western Sea, by lnverriefs and Fort William; by which means Ships, going to or coming from Ireland and the Weft of England, in the Baltic Trade, will have a safe passage, without being exposed to the severe gales and heavy seas from the Western Ocean, when going Northward or coming Southward; and Vessels engaged in trade from these Ports, with the Eastern Coasts of England and Scotland, and vice verfd, will be greatly benefited, efpe-

cially in time of War, by passing through this Canal instead of going round by the Land’s End:

That the said Work might have been profitable to the Company, if they had made the Canal of small dimensions j but they were desirous that it might accommodate large Vessels engaged in Foreign Trade, by which the expence was so much increased as to leave but small prospect of ^ny reasonable interest for the money expended, unless by the good effects it shall produce to the Community, the traffic by the said Canal shall very much increase.

The Witness further produced a Statement to the Committee, by which it appeared, that the Tolls allowed to be taken on the said Canal will probably amount to near £. 9,000 annually, when the Canal shall be completed.

And the Witness concluded his Evidence by stating.

That, if the said Canal should be flopped and go to ruin for want of further assistance, the Public will not only be deprived of the great advantages which would arise from it to Commerce, to the Fisheries, and to the Improvement of the Western Islands and North-weft Coast of Scotland, but the money which Parliament has already advanced on Loan mull be entirely loft, and the Subscribers to the Canal materially injured.

A Petition of William Jlrmj, John Fauffet, Noble Weir, James Frith, Patrick Dundas, Hugh Dundas, John Fiddis, William Gray don, George John Cooke, George

Moore, and James Moore, all of the County of Fermanagh, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners were sworn upon a Petit Jury at the last Summer Assizes, held at Enniskillen, in and for the County of Fermanagh, to try three persons of the names of John Fletcher, Hugh Keys, and James Sharpe, for the murder of one Nicholas Morris; and that the principal witnesses, produced on the part of the Crown, to prove the said crime against the persons charged, were Cormick Maguire and James M’Nab, two persons whose characters were well

known to the Petitioners, and to moll of the persons in their neighbourhood who usually compose the Petit Jury; and that Rewards had been offered by the Government of the Country, by Proclamation, and by the Gentlemen of the County, to an amount of nearly . 8oo. for prosecuting to conviction any of the persons concerned , in the said ■,murderj notwithstanding which, several months had elapsed

before any information was given relative thereto by the said M’Nab and Maguire, or any person whatsoever; and that the said M’Nab and Maguire, induced by the said Reward (as the Petitioners think they have a right to presume) came forward, and made examinations against the persons aforesaid; and, on the said trial, on which the Petitioners were the Jury, proved that they were in afield at fonie distance from the place where the murder was committed, at the time when the fatne was perpetrated; and that when the persons who perpetrated the fame were beating and battering with sticks and Hones the said deceased Nicholas Morris, they the said witnesses had heard the deceased call upon the Prisoners (who were so tried by the Petitioners) by name, net to kill him, and that they heard other words pass from the deceased; but neither they, nor any Witness for the Crown, identified the Prisoners as having been present, either from free or voice; and that it appeared to the Petitioners,'that none of the said Prisoners had lied for or on account of the said murder; that they had been admitted to bail at the preceding Assizes, and had surrendered in discharge of their Bail, and each of the said Prisoners gave moll respectable testimony of their good moral and religious character; and that the Petitioners considered themselves, under thebleffcdConftitution under which they live, and which they have armed to support and defend, as the Judges not only of the matter of fact which they were sworn to try, but the credit of the Witnesses produced to prove that fact; and that the Honourable Judge Fox,who prelided on that trial, after recapitulating the evidence to them, charged them very llrongly to find the Prisoners guilty; and that when the Petitioners had retired to their room, and came to weigh the evidence, and the credit of the Witnesses, they were of opinion that the evidence was not entitled to such credit from them, nor was there such certainty in their account astojuftify a verdict of Guilty, and their taking away the lives of three men; and that the Petitioners are ready to lay a note of the evidence before Parliament, to justify their verdict, if they are permitted to do so; and that when the Petitioners delivered their verdict, the said Honourable Judge expressed much dissatisfaction thereat; and that on the next morning, when the Court was full, the said Honourable Judge Fox called on the Clerk of the Crown to furnish him with a List of the names of the Petitioners, which having received, he caused the whole of the Grand Inquest of the County, then sworn, and fitting in their room on the public business, to be called into the Court House, when, in the face of the whole County, the said Honourable Judge Fox stigmatized the Petitioners as men not worthy to be believed on their oaths, and as unfit ever again to act in the capacity of Jurors, and cautioned the said Grand Jury and others never thereafter to hold communion or intercourse with them; that he ordered the Clerk of the Crown to deliver in a list of their names to every succeeding Judge as men unfit to be Jurors, that they might prevent their serving as such thereafter; and that he ordered the High and Under Sheriff to deliver a list of their names to the succeeding Sheriff, with a direction to hand them down from Sheriff to Sheriff as branded with the infamy of a verdict, which was for ever to render them unworthy of credit, and ordered that their names should be publicly potted up as such in the Grand Jury-room; and that the Petitioners, though not men of large Estates, arc men of substance, and have heretofore enjoyed not only good, but they think they may add high, characters for honesty and integrity among their neighbours, and in the County in general, an inheritance more dear to them to hand unful-lied to their children than any adventitious gift of fortune; and that, valuing their characters above all human enjoyments, they have felt-debased in their own eyes until they shall have had a public investigarion of their conduct, and reparation for what they conceive to be the greatest of all possible injuries; And therefore praying the House to take the premilcs into their consideration, and permit the Petitioners to prove the fame at the Bar of the House, and thereupon to afford liich satisfaClion to the Petitioners as the justice and merits of their case, and the conduct of the said Judge to them, may entitle them, and as to the House shall lcem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

to be at the proper place before the time appointed, with such attendants as usual, and dressed as well as became the Petitioner’s fortune, and with which the Judges on the Spring Circuit had not found any fault; and that the Petitioner resides near the extremity of the County mod distant from where the Judges were to enter it, and was therefore obliged to set out from his own house the day before the day on which the Judges were to enter the fame, and to ileep at a small and indifferent Inn in the Village of Newtown Butler, which can only afford accommodation

for two or three persons, and that very indifferent, on earthen floors, from which circumstances the Petitioner could not expect the Gentlemen of the County to submit to such accommodation, merely to be in his posse to receive the Judges; and that, in compliance with the Petitioner’s requett, a number of Gentlemen of the County did meet the Judges some miles from the County Town, on the day of their arrival; and that the Petitioner would have been at the Bounds of the County at lead half an hour before;the time appointed by Mr. Justice , but he, having come at an earlier hour than he had appointed, had advanced into the Petitioner’s Bailiwick about two miles before the Petitioner and his attendants came up; and that the Petitioner, on meeting the Judges, went up, with his hat off, to apologize, and mention, the caul'e of his not being at the Bounds of the County when they arrived, when the Honourable Justice Fox, in the mod insulting manner, without noticing the Petitioner, ordered his postilion to drive on; and that, on going into the Court-house (though the Judge was in his riding dress, in boots, &c.) after the Petitioner going to his carriage to wait on him, on his coming out he rushed by the Petitioner in a mod violent manner, ordering the Petitioner, in the mod insulting language, to take off his hat; and that, although the Petitioner had paid him every respect as aforesaid, and he and his Brother Judge had honoured the Petitioner with their company at dinner on the preceding day, the said Honourable Judge Fox,in his charge to the Grand Jury, delivered in the face of the County, used the mod gross and degrading language to the Petitioner, such as had never before been addressed to him (the Petitioner then aiding as High Sheriff) for not having come to meet him on his entering the Bounds of the County, and charged the Petitioner, in the grossed manner, with farming out to hire his Bailiwick, which the Petitioner never did, and concluded by imposing on the Petitioner a fine of for not meeting him as aforesaid; and that the Petitioner humbly conceives, that, although his not being at the Bounds of the County to meet the Judge on his entrance was an omission, it was owing to the Judge being so much earlier than the time he had appointed, which may appear by the affidavit of Mr. George Bell, the person the Petitioner sent to the County of Cavan (in place of his Sub-sheriff, who was then indisposed, and isfincedead) to wait on the Judges in his name, and receive their commands, and particularly to know the hour at which the Petitioner should be in waiting for them; these circumstances considered, the Petitioner truds it was not such a crime as to merit opprobrious censure, and so heavy a fine; and that the Petitioner feels degraded and abused in the eyes of his country, so long as the injury he has dated remains unre-dressed; and that the Petitioner can verify on oath the truth of the foregoing Petition: And therefore praying the House to afford the Petitioner fuchredrefs as to judice may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Trustees of The British Museum being British offered to be presented to the House; Museum

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty’s eution’ command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, hav- '

ing been informed of the contents of the said Petition, j

recommends it to the confederation of the House. j

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That His Majesty having been graciously pleased to order the valuable Egyptian Amtiquiries, which were acquired by His Majesty’s victorious arms during the late Expedition to Egypt, to be deposited in The British Museum, the Petitioners provided temporary coverings for their, preservation, which, nevertheless, are found to be insufficient for protecting them from the injury of the weather; and it is apprehended that, unless better secured, they may in a short time be materially defaced, whereby His,

Majesty’s gracious intentions will be frustrated, to the detriment of Science, and the disparagement of these memorable Trophies of National Glory; and that the Peti-

tioners, desirous to prevent consequences so much to be regretted, have caused a Plan and Estimate to be prepared of an addition to the present Building, for the purpose of effectually preserving these valuable Monuments in a suitable manner, as well as for the reception of other important specimens of the fine Arts already in their possession, and to which, it is hoped, that material additions may be made from time to time; but, as the Petitioners are unable to proceed in the execution of so necessary a work, which, upon the mod exact computation, cannot be completed at a less expence than yf. 16,000, without the Public Aid, they submit the whole matter to the wiidom and munificence of Parliament, conceiving that they should be wanting to the Public in the execution of the trust with which they have been invested, if they omitted to represent these circumstances, in confidence that an Institution so honourable to this Country will never fail to receive the support of the Legifiaturc.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Giles reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Members of the society for bettering the Condition of the Poor, was referred; and who were empowered to report the matter of the said Petition, as it should appear to them, with their Observations thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had made several Observations thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it iu at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the matter to them referred; and have agreed to the following Report:

Sir Walter Farqukar, m. 0. having been examined, informed Your Committee, That to his knowledge and experience, the Infectious Fever was very prevalent in London, particularly among the poorer parts in confined lituations: That from information, which he repeatedly had, and on which he could rely, he had reason to believe that more than 3,000 persons have annually died of it in and about London :—That there can be no doubt that a House for receiving Patients in the Fever, would prevent the spreading the infection; particularly if the houses from which the patients are removed, were properly cleaned and white-washed, and still more so if the bed-cloaths, and also the Patients cloaths, were burnt immediately.—That he had known the mod fatal consequences follow from the neglect of this precaution, even in the instance of a tingle article coming from an infected person.—That he did not conceive that an Establishment, on a sufficient scale to answer those beneficial purposes, could be formed in the Metropolis without public aid, and had no scruple to say, that he believed it impossible.—That the Infection is likely to be generally communicated, by the necessary intercourse subsisting between servants and other members of large families, with persons in the lower classes of life, among whom the I nfectious Fever more commonly prevails.—-That he has known repeated instances of its being so communicated to persons in the higher classes of life, particularly among children, and has found it necessary to lay it down as a rule in families where he is consulted, that the nurses should never have any communication with friends in their own houses, or with others they may casually meet.—That there is good reason to hope, that by the judicious, diligent, and persevering efforts of such an Institution as has been alluded to, that the Infectious Fever may be very considerably diminished, and even in the end almost entirely extirpated from the Metropolis.—And, that the extinction of the Infectious Fever in the Metropolis, would very greatly tend to prevent its taking place in those parts of the country which have a communication with it, more especially as the Fever generally remains lurking in the constitution for feme time before it prevents the patient from travelling, or following his usual occupations.—That it is of great importance in the cure of these Fevers, to attend to them in an early stage; and general attention cannot be given to Patients so infected in the wide extent of the Metropolis, except by the establishment of an Institution upon a considerable scale, and very carefully directed, so as to be capable of receiving all the infected persons who may apply. —That the Poor, when in their own houses, labouring under the Infectious Fever, must always be attended Vo l.

by their friends with hazard; and, though some peculiar constitutions may escape, in general the attendance mull be highly dangerous.

Maxwell Garthjhore,m. d. having been examined, also

informed Your Committee,—That an Institution to prevent the spreading of contagious malignant Fevers, has been established within these three years in Road,

which, although upon a very contracted scale, previous to February last received 325 Fever Patients, of whom 289 have been dismissed cured, and the houses of many of them, and others, purified, white-washed, and cleansed j 29 died, and 7 then remained in the House.—That he does not think the present Establishment sufficiently extensive, to remedy the evil of the Infectious Fever in the Metropolis.—That a Public Institution would afford means both of preventing and curing the Infectious Fever, which cannot be practised in the houses of the poorer classes of society; but that he is of opinion that a Public Institution, of sufficient extent to remedy the evil in the Metropolis, cannot be established by private subscription unassisted by public aid.—That it is of great importance that the Infectious Fever should be attended to in its early stages; and that he believes that not one case was ever taken into this Institution in an early stage, which was not soon recovered, it being a disorder the prevention and cure of which are perfectly well understood.—That the Infectious Fever has prevailed for along course of years in some of the crouded parts of the Metropolis, in a more or less degree, according to seasons and circumstances.

Thomas Bernard, Esquire, having been examined, like-wife informed Your Committee, That the London Fever Hospital in Gray’s-Inn-Lane, was established in May 1801, and a House of Recovery opened in Gray's*lnn-Lane in February 1802.—That great exertions have been made in every possible way to obtain Subscriptions, and yet the present Funds are not equal to the maintaining that small House on the present scale.—That the whole sum which has been raised by Donations and Subscriptions, has amounted to £.4,378; the annual eXpences of the House are between £.600 and £.700; and that the House is not adequate to one-tenth part of the Patients who want relief, as it contains only 16 beds.—Finding that this Establishment will not be adequate to me purpose, the Society have begun railing a Fund of £. 3.000, and £. 1,600 has already been subscribed, upon e ndition that Parliament would grant such a Sum as, together with those Subscriptions, would prove effectual to the defined object.

Upon the whole, Your Committee find that the Infectious Fever has been long prevalent among the Poor of London, and that above 3,000 persons have, on an average, annually died of it within the Bills of Mortality.

This evil appears to Your Committee to have continued for want of some regular System being adopted to check its progress, and to purify the houses and other buildings in which it has prevailed.—In May 1801, an Institution for the Cure and Prevention of Infectious Fevers in the Metropolis was established by the Society for bettering the Condition of the Poor; and in February 1802, a London House of Recovery was opened, in which, although it contains no more than 16 beds, upwards of 320 Fever Patients have already been cured.

This Establishment has been hitherto supported by the Contributions and Subscriptions of Individuals, and nearly the whole of £.4,000, so collected, has been expended upon it. The extent of the Institution appears to Your Committee insufficient for the attainment of its object; and although great exertions have been used, it has not been found practicable to raise, by private Subscriptions, Funds large enough to increase or support it, more especially as it is efientially necessary to destroy the cloaths of the Patients, and purify the houses in which they have been attacked by the complaint. In the expectation that, towards an object of so much National Importance, aid might be afforded by the Legislature, a sum of £. 1,600 has been subscribed by several Individuals, upon the condition of such assistance being first received. The Institution cannot, therefore,- have the benefit of this Bounty, without it is also supported by Parliament: and, upon the whole, it appears to Your Committee, That the object of the Petition

Mr. Henry Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as folio wet h; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury be authorized to contract with any person or persons for the purchase of any number of Tickets to be drawn in three Lotteries, not exceeding Eighty Thousand, subject to such Discount for Prompt Payment, and under such Rules and Regulations as the said Lords Commissioners of the Treasury shall think proper:

That a sum, not exceeding the amount of Ten Pounds for each Ticket so fold, shall be distributed into Prizes, for the benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lotteries, which Prizes shall be charged upon the Aids and Supplies granted in this Sellionof Parliament for Great Britain and Ireland, for the service of the year 1804, and be paid at the Bank of Englin money, to the Proprietors, upon demand, within two months after the drawing of each of the said Lotteries, or as soon after as certificates can be made out, without any deduction whatsoever:

That all the money arising by the sale of such Tickets shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer at Westminster, and applied, from time to time, to such fer-

vices, for Great Britain and Ireland, as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament, in the proportion of two-thirds for Great Britain, and one-third for Ireland.

Lord Viscount Marsham also acquainted the House, That the said Select Committee had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the poll, on the first of which days there was a considerable majority of votes in favour of William Mainw Esquire, the Sheriff,

Robert Albion Cox, Esquire, and Sir William Knight, wilfully, knowingly, and corruptly, did admit to poll for Sir Francis Burdett, Baronet, upwards of three hundred persons, claiming to. vote under a fiditious right, as Proprietors of a Mill purported to be situate in the Pari 111 of IJlevjorth, and called The Good Intent Mill, by which means a colourable majority was obtained in favour of Sir Francis Burdett, who was thereby returned as having the greatest number of legal votes.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, on the fifteenth day, towards the close of the poll, after such majority was established, they rejected persons tendering their votes under the fame circum (lances.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Sheriff, at the poll, acted in a judicial capacity, byadmitting counsel to argue the validity of votes, and by deciding, in feme instances, on the validity of such votes that in other instances, they refilled to decide on the validity of votes, which were objected to, and stated, that they would admit any persons to poll who would take the Oaths, declaring themselves to be only Ministerial Officers, thereby acting in a manner contradictory to their practice in other cases, and in flagrant violation of their duty.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the obvious tendency of their conduct was to admit Persons having no right, to poll, and to afford the greatest encouragement to perjury.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further confederation upon Tommorrow Sevennight, the 17 th day of this instant July.

Ordered, That the said Report be printed for the Members of the House.

Ordered, That so much of the Minutes of the Evidence, taken before the said Select Committee, as relates to the matters contained in the said Report, be laid before this House.

A MESSAGE by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Mountague, Esquire, being examined, said, That by a recent survey of the Poultry Compter in the City of London, it has been found to be in such a Rate of decay, as to become inadequate to the (afe custody of the Debtors and Prisoners therein confined, and extremely dangerous as well to the lives of the said Debtors and Prisoners, as to other persons resorting thereto; and that, from the above circum-stances, the Petitioners apprehend it may become indispen-sably necessary to remove the Debtors and Prisoners in the -said Compter to some other place of confinement for safe custody, during the time that may be requisite for the rebuilding of the said Compter.

A Petition of Cyprian Whillock, of New Brentford, Inn- petition of keeper, was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting Cyprian forth. That the Petitioner, on the 6th instant, was committed to Prison, by the Order of the House, upon a discharged. charge of prevarication in his Evidence before the Committee of the House fitting to. decide upon the election of a Knight of the Shire for the County of Middlesex; and that he humbly implores the forgivenels of the House for the said offence, and hopes that the House will impute his crime to ignorance and the embarrassment of his mind, and not to any premeditated design taimpose upon, mislead, or treat with difrespect, the said Committee; and that the Petitioner’s business and concerns are very much injured by his absence from home, and without he is speedily permitted to return thither, he must be utterly ruined: And therefore praying. That the House will accept his most humble submission, and this declaration of his sincere and unfeigned contrition, and be pleased to order -his discharge, on payment of his fees.

the Bar of this House, upon Wednesday next, in order to j

his being discharged.
