Cyprian IVhillock,

A Select Committee of this House. appointed to try and determine the merits of the Middlesex Election, has reported. That you, being called as a Witr.els before the said Committee, were guilty of gross pievarication j for ■which offence they committed you to the custody of the Serjeant at Arms, and this House did further commit you to His Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate.

The matter under examination by the Committee, when you were called upon to giv»c evidence, was the Charge of Treating; a practice which, according to the language of the Law, is " in violation of the freedom due to the " tlcftion of the Reprefer.tatuvs for the Commons, to the w great scandal of the Kingdom, ddhom.mable and de-" strublive to the Conflituti n of Parli cnenis."

Your occupation in life, and vom relidence at the time of the election, qualified yoj to'have guen important testimony upon this Chuige; the points to which you were interrogated were such as mu!i have fallen within your own knowledge; and yet, in so plain a matter, rcgaullefs of the reverence due to the Authority of this Home, and reg.ard-less also of the h.lemnity of the oath which you had taken, you appear to have incurred the heavy guilt of wiifudy prevaricating before God and y >ur Countiy.

For this your offence you l ave tnoft justly suffered disgrace and imprisonment: but this House, tonfiJering 'he ' penitence you have since expteffed, and hoping alto, that the example of your punishment may fulHciently enl'ure a better execution of the Writ issued for a new election, has ordered that you be now discharged r And you are discharged accordingly, paying your Fees.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that so much of an Act of the thirty-first year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as regulates the Prices at which British Corn, Grain, Malt, Meal, or Flour, may be exported, except to Ireland, and Foreign Corn, Grain, Meal, and Flour, imported, except from Ireland; and also the Duties and Bounties payable thereon, be repealed, except any Duty payable on any Foreign Corn or Grain, in respect of the warehousing thereof.

Rofolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that the Importation of Cprn, Grain, Meal, and Flour, be regulated by the Average Price of Corn,

Grain, and Oatmeal, in the whole of the twelve Maritime Distrids in England and Wales, and in the whole of the four Maritime Distrids in Scotland-, and that the Exportation of Corn, Grain, Meal, Flour, and Biscuit, be regulated by the Average Price of Corn and Grain in the whole of the said Distrids in England and Wales, and in Scotland, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Bounties herein after mentioned be allowed on all Corn, Grain, Malt, and Flour, exported from Great Britain; that is to say,

may be imported into Ireland from Foreign parts on the second Low Duties specified in the Schedules, the Exportation of Corn and Grain of growth, or Meal or Flour made thereof, should be permitted from Ireland to Great Britain.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr.. Smith and Mr. Simeon:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making further Regulations for the better Collection and Security of His Majesty's Revenue of Customs and Excise in Ireland, and for preventing Frauds therein; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to permit, until the twenty*fifth day of March one thousand eight hundred and five, the warehousing of Spirits in Ireland for Exportation; for charging a Duty on the lame when taken out for Home Consumption; and to regulate the Exportation to Great Britain of such Spirits as shall not be warehoused; without any Amendment: And also, '

The Lords1 have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue, until the twenty-ninth day of September one thousand eight hundred and five, several Acts for the better Collection and Security of His Majesty’s Revenue in Ireland, and for preventing Frauds therein; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The Order of the day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to regulate the Importation and Exportation of Corn, and the Bounties and Duties payable thereon.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir ‘Thomas Charles Bunbury took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir 'Thomas Charles Bunbury reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Sir Thomas Charles Bilnbury accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee bad made to the Bill, and which they had directed bim to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were once read throughout; and then a second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House: And an Amendment was made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be in-grofied.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the third time Tomorrow.

And then the House adjourned till Tommorrow Morning, Ten of the clock.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty: Where His Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the Public Bill following;

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain sum of Money out of the Consolidated Fund of Great Britain t and for applying a certain sum of Money therein mentioned for the service of Great Britain, for the year one thousand x1 eight

His Malay’s After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a moll

Speech. Gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Par—

' liament, as followeth; vi

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Before I put an end to the present Session of Parliament,

I am detirous of expressing My entire approbation of the zeal and assiduity with which you have applied yourselves to the great objects of public concern which have come under your consideration.

You have wifely continued to direct your attention to the encouragement and improvement of that respectable and powerful Volunteer Force which the ardour and spirit of My Subjects have enabled me to establish to an extent hitherto unexampled: You have at the same time endeavoured to combine an additional Establishment for Our domestic Defence with the means of augmenting Our liegular Army, and of maintaining it on such a scale as may be proportioned to the circumstances of the times, and to the rank which this Country ought ever to hold among the Powers of Europe.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

You are entitled to My warmest acknowledgments for the fresh proof which you have given Me of your constant and affectionate attachment to My Person and Family, and your regard to the Honour and Dignity of My Crown, by the liberal provision which you have made for the Payment of the Debt on My Civil List Revenues, and for furnishing me with the additional means of defraying the increase which has unavoidably taken, place in different branches of My Expenditure.

I mult also return you My warmest thanks for the ex-tensive provision which you have made for the exigencies of the Public Service; and especially for the just and prudent attention which you have shewn to true economy, and to the permanent credit and welfare of the Country, by the great exertions you have made for preventing, as far a*

' possible, the accumulation of Debt, and for railing so large a proportion of the Expences of the War within the year.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have now only to recommend to you, to carry into your . respective Counties the fame zeal for the Public Interest which has guided all your proceedings. It will be your particular duty to inculcate, on the minds of all classes of My Subjects, that the preservation of all that is most dear to them requires the continuance of their unremitted exertions for the National Defence.

The preparations which the Enemy has long been forming for the declared purpose of invading this Kingdom are daily augmented, and the attempt appears to have been delayed only with the view of procuring additional means -for carrying it into execution.

Relying on the Ikill, valour, and discipline of my Naval and Military Force, aided by the voluntary zeal and native courage of My People, I look with confidence to the issue of this great conflict; and I doubt not, that it will terminate, under the Blefiing of Providence, not only in repelling the danger of the moment, but in establishing, in the eyes of Foreign Nations, the security of this Country on a basis never to be lhaken.

; In addition-to this first and great object, I entertain the animating hope that the benefits to be derived from Our successful exertions will not be confined within Ourselves; but that, by their example and their consequences, they may lead to the re-establishment of such a system in , as may refeue it from the precarious state to which it is reduced; and may finally raise an effectual barrier against the unbounded schemes of aggrandizement and ambition which threaten every independent Nation that yet remains on the Continent.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Parliament command, feid, prorogued.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday, the 4th day of September next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday, the 4th day of September next.

(fro. COPY ofaCONVENTION between His Britannic Majesty and the King of Sweden, signed on the 25th July 1803.

50 Decembris.; —

Ills Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and his Majesty the King of Sweden, being equally desirous ol [.romoting the good understanding which happily subsists between them, and of preventing the recurrence of those differences which have heretofore arisen respecting the Eleventh Article of the Treaty of Alliance concluded and signed at Whitehall, on the 21ft day of October 1661, have named and authorized for that purpose, viz. His Britannic Majesty, the Right honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson Lord Httwkesbury, one of His said Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, and His Principal Secretary of State for the Foreign Department; and his Swedi/h Majesty, George Uldric Baron de Silverhjelm his Envoy Extraordinary and Miniller Plenipotentiary to His Britannic Majesty, and Knight of the Order of the Polar Star who, after having duly communicated to each other their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article iff. In the event of one of the contracting Parties being heutral during a War, in which the other contracting Party may be belligerent, the Vtfiels of the neutral Party shall not carry to the Enemy or Enemies of the belligerent Party, Money, Arms, or Bombs toith their Fufees and other Appurtenances, Fire Balls, Gunpowder, Matches, Cannon Balls, Spears, Lances, Pikes, Halberts, Gans, Mortars, Petards, Grenadoes, Musket-Rests, Bandaliers, Saltpetre, Muskets, Musket Bullets, Helmets, Head-pieces, Breast-plates, Coats ‘ of Mail, commonly called CuirafTes, and the like kind of Arms, or

Troops, Ilorfes, or any thing necessary for the equipment of Cavalry, or Pistols, Belts, or any other lniiruments of War, or Ships of War, and Guard Ships, nor any manujattured articles immediately firving for the equipment of the fame, under the penalty, that if either of the contracting Parties shall seize the fame, these articles shall be liable to tonfifealion.

Article 2d.—The Cruizers of the Belligerent Power shall exercise the right of bringing in the Ships of the Neutral going to the Ports of an Enemy, laden with cargoes of Proiifivns, or with cargoes of Pitch, Tar, Hempi and generally all vnmamjattured articles whatever seeing for the equipment of Ships of all descriptions, and likewise all manufactured articles serving for the equipment of Merchant Vessels (Herrings, Iron in Bars, Steel, Rose-Copper, Brass, and Brals Wire, Deal Planks, not being of Oak, and Spars, however, excepted); and if

the Cargoes so exported in the bottoms of the Neutral Power are the produce of the Territories of the said Neutral Power, and going on account of the Subjects thereof, the Belligerent Power shall in that case exercise the right of purchasing them, upon condition of paying a profit of ten per-centum upon a fair Invoice price, or the fair Market-price in England or in Sweden, respecHively, at the option of the Owner, with an indemnification for detention, and necessary expences.

Article 3d.—If the Cargoes specified in the preceding Article (not being Enemy's property) are proceecing with a profefied destination to the Ports of a Neutral Country, and are brought in under suspicion that their true destination is to the Ports of the Enemy, and it shall turn out upon due enquiry that they were really bound to Neutral Ports, they shall be at liberty to pursue their Voyages after being indemnified for their detention and necessary Expences, unless the Government of the Belligerent Country, from a reasonable appreben-fion of their falling into the hands of the Enemy, flioald de/ire to purchase them, in which case the full price should be paid which they would have obtained in the Ports of the Neutral Country to which they were going, with an indemnification for detention, and necessary expences.

Article 4th.—Herrings, Iron in Bars, Steel, Rose-Copper, Brass, and Brass Wire, Deal Planks, not being of Oak, and Spars, shall not be liable to Confiscation or Pre-emption on the part of the Belligerent Power, but shall be permitted to pass free in the Ships of the Neutral Country, provided that they are not Enemy's property.

Article 5th.—The present Convention shall be ratified by His Britannic Majesty, and by his Swedi/h Majesty, and the Ratifications exchanged at London in the space of two months, or sooner if it can be done.

In witness whereof, We, the undersigned Plenipotentiaries of His Britannic Majesty, and of his Swedi/h Majesty, have signed the present Convention; and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at London, the twenty-fifth day of July 1803.

(l. s,) Haivke/bury. (l. s.) Joran Uldric Silverhjelm.

Memorandum:

A Negociation is on foot, and in progress to conclusion, with the Grand Canal Company, for making and maintaining a Navigation upon the River Shannon, from Lough Derg to Lough Ree, upon a very low rate of Toll. The expence will amount to about £.40,000.

OBSERVATIONS.

This Navigation, by the Act of 1800, became vested in the Directors of all Works relating to Inland Navigation, besides the sum dated to have been expended by the Board. —£. 8,000, a saving upon their Tolls, and £. 3,964. 2 s. 9 d. since collected under this Board for Tolls, have alf6 been applied to the repairs and improvement of the Navigation from the Sea into Loughneagh.

This Navigation, by the Act of 1800, became vested in the Directors of all Works relating to Inland Navigation; the sum dated to have been expended by the Board is for the actual restoring of the Navigation, the Works having been in ruins, and the Navigation abandoned. The Maghery Cut, when perfeded, will open a pafi'age into Loughneagh from the Blackwater, avoiding the Bar of that River.

The Board, by Agreement entered into with the Limerick Navigation Company, have undertaken to execute the Works by their own Engineers, and to complete this Navigation, upon condition of a very material reduction of the Tolls; by Contract executed 24th of June 1803.

(a) This Grant is for a completion of the Canal from Dublin to the extremity of the Summit Level at or near Coolnahay, in the County of Wedmeath; and for the execution of their Works at Dublin, and adjoining the Liti'ey, and for a reduction of their Tolls upon the whole extent of that Navigation 5 by Contract executed 3d of November 1801.

(b) £■ 20,000 of this Grant is upon condition of a reduction of the Tolls of this Navigation, and the remainder is for tha completion of the Navigation from A thy in the Queen's County, to the deep Water below the Scarrs at St. Mullins; by Contract executed 8th of February 1^03.

This Account is properly and correctly dated, supported by sufficient Receipts and Vouchers, and by the Evidence of the Superintendent Klagidrate, the Chief Condable, and the Secretary. The Lord Mayor of Dublin has inspected the Constables and Watch, and reports veiy favourably on their order, appointment, and sufficiency.

Under the head of Law-Charges are contained the Bills of Cods of the Law Agent, who is also Secretary to the Superintendent Magistrate*

We have now been induced to allow the Charges under this head, as any disallowances made in it mud fall 011 the Superintendent Magistrate, who has actually paid the amount of the Bills, and who thought himself authorized to do so, as the Charges had formerly been acquiesced in, and the Bills were produced to him, taxed by the proper Officers.

We have here to observe, that for want of a sufficient check before the Taxing Officers (as no person appears on the part of the Public at, the Taxation of Bills of Colts, as is usual between Agent and Client) the Bills of Cods of Accountants appear to us extremely expense, and not proportionally beneficial to the Public. In the present instance, a double inconvenience has ensued, as the Superintendent Magistrate has declared, that the heavy expence incurred in his Law Proceedings has prevented him from indituting Profixutlous which he thought would have been useful to the Police of the City.

The COMMITTEE appointed to consider of* the Charge upon llis Majesty s Civil List Revenue } and who were directed to report the fame, together with their Opinion, to the house; and to whom the several Accounts presented to the house by Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command,

on the 12th day of this instant March, have been referred;-----

Have proceeded in the Examination of the several Mattefrs teferred to them; and have agreed upon the following Report.

The Nature of the Charge upon His Majesty’s Civil List Revenue, the Arrangement by which it is distributed into several Classes, and the Comparison of the Lftimate for each, as laid before Parliament in the year 1786, with the actual Charge in every subsequent year, have been already lo fully stated in the Reports of the Select Committees appointed to consider this subject, in the two last years, that Your Committee conceive it will only be necessary for them to incorporate the Accounts of the last year, with those of the preceding, in the Tables already prepared; in order to enable the house to appreciate the causes of the Excels which has led to an Annual accumulation of Debt; after adverting to such items in the Accounts now laid before the house as appear to deserve particular notice; and subjoiuing, as they are required to do, their Opinion upon the whole.

They have accordingly.stated in the Appendix to their Report,—

1. An Account of the Charge of the Civil List as estimated in 1786, and the Charge of the fame in the year ending January 5th 1803, with the Increase and Dccrease thereof; which it is thought fit to exhibit again in the form in which it is presented to Parliament in the present year; as being now prepared from actual instead Of, in some inltance?, from estimated Charges, it affords a more accurate Statement than that which was presented in the last year, and printed in the Report of that Committee.

2. A fnnilar Account, made up to the 5th January last.

3. Comparative Account of the Particulars of Charge in each Class, atul in each year, from 1786 to the present, and as then estimated: that of the year 1802 being corrected from the Account, Appendix

(A.)

4. An Abstract of the general Amount of Charge in each year, from the year 17S6 to the present; compared in like manner wdth the Estimate then made, as applicable to each.

5. An Account of the Debt of llis Majesty’s Civil List on 5th January last, as laid before the house by llis Majesty’s Command.

6. An Account of the Payments which had been made on 5th

January 1804, in discharge of the Debt of the Civil List on the 5th January 1802; shewing the Excels or Diminution of the Charges paid, as compared with the Estimate of the Debt laid before Parliament.

7. A11 Account of the manner in which the Debt has arisen, from 5th January 1802 to the 5th January 1804; and the actual Amount iff the Deficiency, after taking credit for the Auxiliary Funds granted by Parliament.

From an examination of these Documents, it will appear, that, as hiis been noticed in the preceding Reports, the Excess of Expenditure beyond the Estimate is to be found, almost exelufively, in the Third snd Fourth Classes, and the head of Occasional Payments/’

The first of the lc comprizes the regular Establiftnnent of the whole Diplomatic Cody, the Charge of which for the year 1802, will be found to exceed the Estimate of 1786, by the sum of £. 19,045. 145. 2^d. and that for the year 1803, by the sum of £. 36,084. 3 s. io| d.

It was observed in the Report of last year, that 44 the Charge of 44 this Class, had always during the years of Peace, in some degree " exceeded the Estimate; that the increase had been progressive, being 44 in the first year above £.4,000, amounting in 1790 to near * £• 17,000, and in 1792, the year immediately preceding the late 44 War, to £< 27,000; that the increase w as truly stated in the Report 44 of 1802, to have arisen partly from some addition to the Allowances 44 of many of the Ambassadors upon the usual establiftnnent, but prin-lt cipally from the occasional appointments of Ministers Plenipoten-n tiary, Envoys Extraordinary, Charge des Affaires, and Secretaries 44 of Legation; for most of whom, as being only temporary, no pro-" vilioivwas profefltdly made in the Eftiinates of 1786:" And it w as also observed, 4* That the rising importance of America since that " year, had also considerably increased the C’haige both in the Diplo- matic and Consulate parts of that Establishment, of which only the 44 appointment of Consul General was included in that Estimate."

4* That in confluence of the late Peace,. which occasioned the

re*appointment of Ministers to France, Spain, and Holland, the n Charge in 1802 had risen to the amount stated; but, that as le-" vcral of the most considerable of these items were taken only for 44 broken parts of the year, and as it might he found necessary licrc- after to revive the Diplomatic relations of this country, in some

44 form or other, with several of those Powers wfith whom they hoi " been discontinued, there seemed no reason to expe^ that, if ll* 44 rates of allowances should continue nearly as in the Account yf 44 1802, the Charge of that Class, on a permanent Peace Establiftnnent, 44 could be taken at a lower scale, if lb low as it actually reached previous to the late War, which* as above noticed, would exceed the H Estimate by at least £. 27,000."

In truth, the appointment of Ministers, in consequence of the Peace having taken place during the courie 6f that year, and their millions having continued through a great part of 1803, and that to the Court of Spain through the whole; while on the other hand, the recommencement of the War may have occasioned some new appointments or increased Allowances to those before existing, neithefr year can be considered entirely on the footing either of a Peace or War establiftnnent; and it may be thought therefore, that the faired mode of obtaining a proper refolt, would be by combining the Charges of the two last years, and taking the average of the whole, which would make the Annual Charge £.98,416; being little more than £.500 above the Charge in 1792, and consequently exceeding the Estimate uk about that amount beyond the £. 27,000 calculated upon in the Report of last year.

The charge of the fourth Class, comprizing, 44 the Approved Bill* 44 of llis Majesty’s Tradelhien, Artificers, and Labourers, for any 44 articles supplied or work done for His Majesty’s Service," which, from its magnitude and general Excess beyond tliA Estimate, particularly attracted the notice of the formcT Committees, does not in the year under consideration, appear to require much additional observation: The Charge indeed of the Lord Chamberlain’s department, which has usually the most exceeded the Estimate, has in the last year been reduced above £. 19,000 below tlrnt of the preceding; while that of the other branches of the lioulehold lays either varied little, or has likewise been reduced, so as on the whole to have amounted to less than it has done in any year since 1799.

In the other subdivision of this Clals, the article of Printing has exceeded that of the preceding year by above £-7,000; still leaving the Charge of the whole Class about £. 14,000 below the amount of the preceding year.

The Charge under the head of " Occasional Payments," which is the third object to which it was proposed to draw* the attention of the house, will be found to have exceeded that of the preceding year, by the sum of £. 52,896, though not to have reached the amount of that of 1801.

The principle articlts in which this Excess has arisen, will appear to be,

Deficiency of Treasury Fees ;—Sheriffs Conviction of Felons, and Overpayments on their Accounts, amounting together loan excels of above £.9,000 ;—Law Churges, £. 15,000 ;—Extra Extraordinaries to Ministers at Foreign Courts, including Reimbursements for expences incurred and Losses fufiuined in His Majesty’s Service abroad, above £.14,000;—Messengers lulls in the Departments of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the War Department, £. 7,000; and Contingencies in the fume, £. 8,000. Some diminution of expence appears to have taken place, but not'in any item of necessary and coniiant Charges..

The whole amount of the Charge of the Civil List in the last year appears to have been £. 1,148,851, exceeding that of the preceding year by £. 48,691; the principle articles of which have been adverted to in the preceding remarks on the Classes, in which the excess has arisen, and which difference would have been still greater, but for the diminution of expence in some of the other CJulies, which it has not been thought necessary particularly to notice. The refnit of the w’hole gives an Excess above the Estimate of 1786, of £. *251,451.

This deficiency naturally leads Your Committee to the consideration of the next object of enquiry, the Debt which has accrued lince the 5th January 1802; the particulars of which, as it now stands, are detailed in the Account in the Appendix; and the occasion of which w’ill be found in the Comparative Statement of Charge of each Class for the last eighteen years.

On this part of the subject in general, Your Committee is led to observe, that from the Statement laid before Parliament in the Report of the year 1802, the inadequacy of the Funds originally defined lor the Charge of the Civil List Expenditure, to the then exilting and probable future demands of that Service, muff have been apparent, and may be considered as having been recognized by the Vote of the house for defraying tire Arrears of Debt incurred up to that period. This deficiency being established, and no provision having since been made by Parliament for increitfing the Funds, or diunnishing the Charge, it is obvious that some accumulation of Debt mull have been expected: As the particulars which have given rife to the present Debt are now submittxd to the consideration of the Iloule, who will thus be enabled to form their own judgment on the result, it may be

Unnecefiary minutely to examine what ground of expectation existed when the former Debt was discharged, as to the probable future deficiency in any given period; but it will be found on referring to the Statement inierted in the Report of 1802, that the Increase of Charge above the Estimate, as flated for the preceding year (adding the fuins then due) amounted to £. 230,031; and it will appear that the average Excess of the two last years, 1802 and 1803, amounts to j£. 227,105 per annum, a 1‘uin not much differing from the former, though it certainly cannot be alfumed that the Amount of Charge for 1801, increased as it was by the payment of turns, to the Amount of £. 51,6*79. which might not, in' the ordinary course, have been included in it, and exceeding, as it did, considerably beyond that Amount, the Charge of the preceding year was necessarily to be taken as the criterion for future years.

On the whole, Your Committee, concurring as they do in the fug-gellions made 1 »y the Committee of lan year, and confirmed by fub-Sequent experience in the propriety of suggesting to Parliament the Adoption of such mealiires as may he adequate to provide for the probable future demands of this Establishment, beg leave to adopt the Observations, with which they concluded their Report.

u On a consideration of the refillt of the whole, Your Committee 4t are of opinion, that the Revenue applicable to the Charge of the " Civil List Expenditure, is become inadequate to the various Services which, in the Estimate of 178G, it was calculated to meet. That, w as this deficiency may obviouily be accounted for by the advance u of price which has taken place fmee that period, on all Articles of Expenditure in which the Establishment of the Household " is concerned, and in the other brandies of a more public nature, 4< by necessary additions to various Articles of Charge, there appears M no ground to expect that the fame Establishment, intended to be 4i provided for by the Estimate in 1786, can be supported in future u without foine considerable additional provision; which Your Committce beg leave to fugged, might be most conveniently made in the following mode: the# arc of opinion, that it would be expe-" dient, in the first place, that a new Ultimate, more adapted to " present circumstances, should now be prepared and laid before " Parliament; that if this was properly formed on such part of the " Fourth Class as respects the Household, it might be reasonally " expected that the future Charge would be provided for, so as to " prevent any Debt arising upon this head.

" They think it might be proper, however, that further regnla-u tions should he adopted, with respect to the Charges comprized in u the second subdivision of that Class, as well as in the Third Class, " and the Occasional Payments, which latter, from the contingent " nature of the various particulars included in it, it is less easy to " provide for by previous estimate. As all these are, in moll of the " Articles, connected with the general Expenditure of the Country, " though, by His Majesty's prerogative, more immediately under His " controul, they are of opinion, that it might be expedient that they " should be submitted annually to the insperition of Parliament; who " would thus be enabled to observe, whether any Excess above the " corrected Estimate had taken place; to Examine the causes and " provide the remedy, either by controuling the expence or taking " measures for its discharge. Considering the extreme uncertainty M of many of these Charges, as well as the necessity of discharging " them by Ready Money Payments, so as not to interfere with the " order intended to be established as to the payment of the other " Claft'es, they wilh further to submit to the wil’dom of the House, u how far it might be prudent to provide annually, by a previous " vote, such a sum as might enlure these Services being provided for " as they arise, subject to an Account of Particulars being laid before " Parliament in each succeeding Session, and liable to their controul, " as in other cases of the dispoliiion of Public Money."

The Fflabliffiment of the Office has necessarily been very much added to, from the great increase of Business; the Salaries have also been increased, which are all charged upon the Fee Fund of the Office: The several Amounts of the Salaries have been returned to Parliament, as well as the Additions that have from time to time been made to them.

J11 addition to thcle, the following Payments are charged upon the Fee Fund, and were formerly paid from other Sources:

Allowances to retired Officers of the Treasury, £. 1,340. Payments of this kind were made in the ffiape of Pensions but of Civil List.

Stationary - - - — about - - - - 1,400. Formerly furnished by the Uftier of the Exchequer.

Additional Land Tax - about - - - - 3,000.

N. B. It does not follow, that an increase of Business should produce a proportionate increase of Fees, as the Correspondence of the

Office makes so material a part of that Increase, for which no Fees are charged.

Contracts for Provisions, &c. or furnished by Commission, used to arise in the Treasury; this branch of Business is now transferred to the Victualling and Transport Board. Considerable Fees were derived from this Source, and are, of course, now loft to the Office.

The Act for regulating the Civil List, and the Act for abolishing Patent and other Offices, under the Commissioners of the Customs, are also causes of the Diminution of the Amount of Treasury Fees.

Note.—In computing the Real Value of the Imports for the Average of Three Years to 25th March 1799, there was 5 per-Cent. added to the Rate of Value of British Manufactures Imported into Ireland, to make up for the Expences luppoled-to be incurred in the Transportation of the Goods from one Country to the other; and 10 per-Cent. was added to the Rate of Value on Foreign Goods Imported through Great Britain, to include the various Expences that occurred from the Tune of landing 111 Great Britain until the Period of Ke-exportaion; together with the British Merchants Profits, but exclusive of the Duties. The Value of the Exports was ejtiniated upon the Principle of the Money which comes into the Country for each Article Exported; it is the Price paid here by the Exporter, increased by the Duty, if any, and all other Charges incurred at Home.

A PLAN for the more easy Admission to The British Museum; being the Regulations now in force:

Appendix, (No. 61.) 3° JuUL

DIRECTIONS respecting the READING ROOM of The British Museum;

Approved 14th January 1803.

THE Reading Room of the Museum is open from Ten till Four, every day: except on Saturdays and Sundays, and for one week at Christmas, Easter, and Whitfuntidc also on Thanksgiving and Fall days.

Persons desirous of Admission are to fend in their Applications, in writing, to the principal Librarian, who will lay the fame before the next General Meeting or Committee of the Trustees. But as it might be dangerous, in so populous a Metropolis as London, tfl admit perfect Strangers, it is expected that every Person who applies, if not known to any Trustee or Officer, should produce a recommendation from some Person of known and approved character.

In all cases which require such dispatch as that time Cannot he allowed for making an application to the Trustees, the principal Librarian, of, in his absence, the Secretary, is empowered to grant a temporary leave, till the next general Meeting or Committee.

Permissions will in general be granted for Three months, and none for a longer term than Six months; and at the expiration of each term, fresh application is to be made for & renewal.

Although the Librarians be fhiclly enjoined to use all possible dispatch in supplying the Readers with the printed Books or Manuscripts they may apply for, yet as in so extensive a Library it may not be possible to find every article immediately, it is recommended to the Readers to allow a reasonable time for the search, especially as to the printed Books.—It is expected that the Library will soon be in such a Rate of arrangement, as to render this intimation superfluous.

No Redder (except in particular cases, at the discretion of the principal Librarian) will be entitled to more than two volumes at a time; but they may be exchanged as often as he may require.

Readers will be allowed to take one or more Extrads from any printed Book or Manuscript; but no whole, or greater part, of a Manuscript is to be transcribed, without a particular leave from the Trustees. The Transcribers are not to lay the paper on which they write on any part of the Book or Manuscript they are using.

No Rerfon is* on any pretence whatever; to write on any part of a printed Book or Manuscript belonging to the Museum; but if any one should observe a defect, or be able to point out an improvement in such Book or Manuscript, he is requested to signify tire fame to the Officer in waiting, who will make proper use of the information.

It may be sufficient merely to suggest that Silence is absolutely re-quilite in a place dedicated to the purposes of ltudy.

British Museum, I 3d July 1804.

Approved 8th June 1804.

PERSONS who wifti to fee the British Museum, will apply at the Assembling Room on any Monday, Wednesday, or Friday, beftveen the Hours of Ten and Two; where each Individual will be required to inferibe his or her Naraei and Place of Abode, in a Book, to be kept for the purpose.

Five Companies, of not more than 15 Persons each, may be admitted in the course of the day; namely, One at each of the hours of 10, 11, 12, 1, and 2.—At each of these hours the directing Officer in waiting shall examine the Entries in the Book; and, if none of the Persons inscribed be exceptionable, he shall consign them to the Attendant whose turn it will be to conduct the Companies through the House.

Should more than 15 Persons inferibe their Names for a given hour, the Supernumeraries will be desired to wait or return at the next hour, when they will be admitted preferably to other Applicants.

And should, in the course of the day, a greater number of Persons apply than can be admitted According to this Regulation, the last Comers shall be allowed to inferibe their Names, and they shall be admitted on the next open day preferably to other Applicants.

The principal Librarian, or, in his absence, the Secretary, shall be allowed to grant Tickets of Admissioi to any particular Companies, of whatever number, not exceeding 15, appointing a certain day and hour, when they will be admitted, without the addition of any of those who apply in the ordinary way. But pot more than one of these Companies shall be appointed for each day; and this shall not be considered as one of the Five Companies admitted in the manner above dated.

N. B. No Money is to be given to the Attendants or Servants.

To Printers, Publishers, and Proprietors of Newspapers, who shall not have raised the Price of their Newspapers above the Price at which the same were respectively sold at and immediately before the time of passing the Act of the Thirty-seventh year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act 44 for granting to His Majesty certain Stamp Duties on the several Matters 44 therein mentioned, and for. better securing the Duties on Certificates, to be 44 taken out by Solicitors, Attornies, and others, practising in certain Courts 44 of Justice in Great Britain/’ and who shall, at one and the same time, produce at the Head Office of Stamps, to be stamped, or shall buy of the Commissioners of the Stamp Duties, Paper stamped with the Duty chargeable on Newspapers, the Duties whereof shall amount to Ten Pounds or upwards, in consideration of prompt or present Payment of such Duty, Sixteen Pounds for every One Hundred Pounds on such Payment, and so in proportion for any

freater or leis Sum, not being under £. 10.; But, if any Printer, Publisher, or roprieior, shall have raised, or shall raise, the Price of his Newspaper above the Price at which the fame was so sold at and immediately before the time of passing of the said Act of the Thirty-seventh year of the Reign of His present Majesty, then and in such Case no more or greater Allowance shall be made, in consideration of such prompt or present Payment, than at the Rate of Four Pounds for every One Hundred Pounds, and so in proportion for any greater or less Sum, not under £. 10.

OBSERVATIONS

ON T H

ABSTRACT of RETURNS made by Overseers of the Poor.

[Continued from the two preceding pages.]

I. —R ET U R N S from Fourteen thousand Six hundred and Eleven Parishes or Places in England and Wales are entered in the AB STRACT of POOR RETURNS, from whence the TOTALS in the foregoing pages are obtained.—Returns from Fourteen thousand Two hundred and Forty Parishes or Places are entered in the Abstra& of the Returns of 1785: Fburteen thousand One hundred and Thirteen in the Abstract of the Returns of 1776.

II. —Three thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-five Parishes or Places maintain all, or part of, their Poor in Workhouses. The Number of Persons so maintained, during the Year ending Easter 1803, was 83,468; and the Expence incurred therein, amounted to £• 1,016,445. 15. 3.; being at the Rate of £. 12. 3. 6£. for each Person maintained in that manner. It appears from the Abfirafi of the Returns of 1776, that there were then 1,970 Workhouses, " capable of accommodating " 89,775 Persons.

HI.—The Number 6f Persons relieved out of Workhouses, was 956,248 (Col. 10. pt. 1/.—Col. 11. and Col. 12.) beftdes 194.052 (Col. 14.) who were not Parishioners. The Expence incurred in the Relief of the Poor not in Workhouses, amounted to £. 3,061,446. 16. 10}. A large Proportion of those, " who were not Parishtoners," appear to have been Vagrants; and, therefore, it is probable, that the Relief given to this Class of Poor could not exceed Two Shillings each, amounting to £. 19,405. 4. o. This Sum being dedu&ed from the above £. 3,061,446. 16. io{. leaves £. 3,042,041. 12. io\.; being at the Rate of £. 3. 3. j\. for each Parishioner relieved " ou t of any Workhouse."

IV. —The Number of Persons relieved in and out of Workhouses, was 1,039,716, besides those " who were not Parishioners." Excluding the Expence supposed to be incurred in the Relief of this Class of Poor, all other Expences, relative to the Maintenance of the Poor (Col. 4. and 5.) amounted to £. 4,093,758. 19. 6{. j being at the Rate of £. 3. 17. 9^. for each Parishioner relieved.

V. —The Resident Population in England and Wales, in the year 1801, appears from the Population Abfiralt to have been 8,872,980; so that the Number of Parishioners relieved from the Poors Rate, appears to be Twelve in *a Hundred of the Resident Population.

The Number of Persons belonging to Friendly Societies, appears to be Eight in a Hundred of the Resident Population.

The Amount of " the Total Money raised by Rates," appears to average at £.0. 12. oj. per Head on the Population.

The Amount of the whole Expenditure on account of the Poor, appears to average at' £. o. 9. 7 J. per Head on the Population.

VI. —The Expenditure in Suits of Law, Removal of Paupers, and Expences of Overseers and other Officers, according to the present Abfintot, ambunts to £. 190,072. 17. of. The Amount of such Expenditure, according to the Abstract of the Returns of 1785 (compnfed'in Columns 11, 12, and 13 of that Abfiradt) was then £. 91,998. 1. 9.

VII. —The Expenditure in purchasing Materials for employing the Poor, according to the present Abstrab*, amounts to £. 47,513. 11. 4i- The Amount of such Expenditure, according to the Abstract of the Returns of 1785, was then £. 15,892. 8. 10.

VIII. —The Poor of Two hundred and Ninety-three Parishes or Places in England and Wales are Rated in the Returns to be farmed, or maintained under Contract.

IX. —The Poor of Seven hundred and Sixty-four Parishes or Places in England and Wales are maintained and employed under the Regulations of special Acts of Parliament.

X. —Five thousand. Four hundred and Twenty-eight Friendly Societies have been enrolled at the Quarter Sessions of the several Counties in England and Wales, purfuaot to the Acts of 330 Geo. III. c. 54. and 35° Geo. III. c. 3 ;—but in this Number are not included the Friendly Societies which may have been enrolled in the County of Devon; —the Holland Division of the County of Lincoln; and the County of Carnarvon ;—the Clerks of the Peace of those Places not having returned any Answer to the Application requefiing them to specify the Number of Friendly Societies which may have been there enrolled pursuant to the said Acts.

XI. —Application having been made to the several Clerks of the Peace, requefiing them to specify " the usual Proportion of the Rated Rental to the Rack Rental," it appears that, according to the Answers received, the Rated Rental amounts on an average to about ‘Thrte-fourthi of the Rack Rental; but many of the Clerks of the Peace have not been able to fiate any thing satisfactory in their Answers to the above Question.

The Rated Rental of each County having been obtained by calculation from the Rates in the Pound returned, and from the Amount of Money there raised— the Total Rated Rental of England and Wales appears to amount to £. 24,129,134; on which the Average Rate in the Pound is £.0. 4. 5$. equal to £ o. 3. 4. on the Rack Rental, estimated according to the Answers received from the Clerks of the Peace.-

In the Returns from Three hundred and Eighty-seven Parishes or Places in England and Wales, the Rate in the Pound is stated on the Rack Rental. The Amount of Money raised by Rates in those Parishes or Places is £.268,381. 2. 9^. The Amount of the Rack Rental, as computed therefrom, is £. 1,679,716. 10. 4{. consequently the Average Rate in the Pound, on this Rental, amounts to £. o. 3. 2j.

It appears however from the Returns made to the Tax-Office for the Year ending April 1804, that the Rental of Real Property in England and Wales amounts to £.34,000,000; not including Mines, Canals, and some other kinds of Real Property, which, with an Allowance for the Deficiencies iocident to Taxation, cannot be efiin)ated at less than £. 4,006,000 per annum. Including this Sum, the fiack Rental of England and Wales, liable to Assessment, amounts to £.38,000,000; on which (the Amount of the Parish Rates being £. 5,348,205.) the actual Rate in the Pound averages at £. o. 10. or nearly (Jnc-seventh part.

XII. —The Area of England and Wales (according to the latefi Authorities) appears to be 58,335 Square Statute Miles, equal to 37.334,400 Statute Acres: Wherefore, the Number of Inhabitants in each Square Mile (containing 640 Acres) average* at 152 Persons.
